articleTitle: Velocity Estimation of an Underwater Vehicle Using Doppler Shift of Positioning Signals
abstract: This paper proposes a method for estimating the moving velocity of underwater vehicles by utilizing the Doppler shift in positioning signals employed for time-of-arrival (ToA) acoustic positioning. The Doppler shift generated in the received signal was measured by resampling, and the moving velocity in global coordinates was estimated by finding the least-squares solution using the Doppler shift generated in the direct wave and the position measured by ToA positioning. Field experiments conducted in a real marine environment demonstrated the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed velocity estimation method.

articleTitle: Entropy Map Based Active Seabed Scanning Method Using Underwater Image Sonar for AUV
abstract: In underwater exploration, where high turbidity and signal attenuation are prevalent, generating 3-dimensional (3D) maps using autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) equipped with image sonar is essential for successfully completing underwater missions. To achieve autonomous underwater mapping for AUV, this paper addresses two-stage seabed scanning method using an autonomous underwater vehicle's image sonar. In the first stage, the AUV generates a 3D volumetric map over a wide area. In the second stage, the entropy-based seabed scanning, is carried out on a interested area using the previous occupancy voxel map. This proposed method was validated through underwater environment simulation experiments. By comparing the residual map entropy and the reconstructed object shape with those obtained using the traditional lawnmower scanning method, the results demonstrate that the proposed method yields better results compared to the conventional approach.

articleTitle: Construction of an Automatic Hypocenter Location System Using Offshore Seismic Network and Distributed Acoustic Sensing Data Using Submarine Cables
abstract: Monitoring seismic activity in subduction zones with huge interplate earthquakes is important. In the Nankai Trough, huge earthquakes with magnitudes of --8 have occurred repeatedly, and seismic observation using an offshore seismic network DONET and distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) measurement have been conducted continuously using submarine cables. DAS measures the temporal change in strain rate along a fiber-optic cable with a meter-scale interval; therefore, high-density observation that cannot be achieved by seismometers can be realized. To monitor seismic activity, we are constructing an automatic hypocenter location system using the DAS and DONET data. In this system, P- and S-wave arrivals of earthquakes are picked automatically using a deep neural network model. After grouping picks, the hypocenter is located by a hypocenter location program with a one-dimensional seismic velocity structure model and that using physics-informed neural networks with a three-dimensional seismic velocity structure model. For located events, the difference in epicenters between this study and the catalog by the Japan Meteorological Agency was ~0.1° (~ 10 km) in many events. The difference is reduced by the program using the three-dimensional model. In this paper, we present the latest results of this automatic hypocenter location system.

articleTitle: Subsea Cable Search and Path Estimation Using Graph SLAM for AUV-Based Inspection
abstract: This research develops a method to efficiently search for and track subsea communication cables using an Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUVs). Inspection of subsea communication cables is a challenging task because they are narrow, making them difficult to detect, have significant route uncertainty that increases with depth, and can be buried for part of their length. The method is based on Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping (SLAM) using an initial map of the cable path that is assumed to be uncertain. Map-guided search patterns are first generated, where successful cable observations update the map using graph-based SLAM. We address the correspondence problem by defining a cable-relative coordinate frame that allows observations to be matched to map locations without the need for distinct cable features. Route uncertainty estimates are based on the location uncertainty of the AUV when observations are made, and physics-based catenary calculations for regions where the cable has not been observed. Updating cable route maps using this approach allows an AUV to efficiently recover a cable route even if it cannot be tracked for part of its length. Here we present the results of simulations that assume a camera-equipped AUV, and demonstrate robust performance of the method on five different cable routes, each with buried sections where the cable is undetectable and different initial cable route uncertainties.

articleTitle: Acoustic Characterization of Gas Seepage at Yam Seep: Exploring the Influence of Methane Concentration on Sound Propagation
abstract: Gas seepage is a common geological phenomenon observed at continental margins. This study aim to monitor and quantify the optimal distance from the source for gas bubbles by conducting acoustic experiments at Yam Seep, located in the southwestern offshore region of Taiwan. This research utilizes a 3D parabolic model to determine the ideal positioning of the source and hydrophone in relation to gas flare locations, thereby investigating the impact of gas flares on sound propagation. Our objective is to address uncertainties in sound propagation resulting from gas emissions, which may aid in mitigating geohazards and improving the monitoring of ocean stability. Additionally, by quantifying the volume of gas emissions, we can gain a deeper understanding of the various geological processes that drive gas seepage, facilitating further exploration of the region's subsurface dynamics and contributing to the comprehension of gas-related geological risks.

articleTitle: Model Predictive Path Integral Docking of Fully Actuated Surface Vessel
abstract: Autonomous docking remains one of the most chal-lenging maneuvers in marine robotics, requiring precise control and robust perception in confined spaces. This paper presents a novel approach integrating Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control with real-time LiDAR-based dock detection for autonomous surface vessel docking. Our framework uniquely combines probabilistic trajectory optimization with a multi-objective cost function that simultaneously considers docking precision, safety constraints, and motion efficiency. The MPPI controller generates optimal trajectories by intelligently sampling control sequences and evaluating their costs based on dynamic clearance requirements, orientation alignment, and target position objectives. We introduce an adaptive dock detection pipeline that processes LiDAR point clouds to extract critical geometric features, enabling real-time updates of docking parameters. The proposed method is extensively validated in a physics-based simulation environment that incorporates realistic sensor noise, vessel dynamics, and environmental constraints. Results demon-strate successful docking from various initial positions while maintaining safe clearances and smooth motion characteristics.

articleTitle: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Collision Avoidance and Path Following of Autonomous Surface Vehicles
abstract: Collision avoidance and path following are critical tasks for Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASV s), particularly in dynamic, multi-agent environments. This paper presents a novel approach to tackling these challenges using Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) for decentralized control. Specifically, we employ the Multi-agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO) [1] algorithm to address the problem of collision avoidance with multiple dynamic obstacles while ensuring effective path following for ASVs [2] [3]. Each agent independently makes navigation decisions without relying on communication with other agents, treating them and any moving objects as dynamic obstacles. In addition to the agents, the environment contains static and random dynamic obstacles, allowing agents to interact with different obstacles during training. This exposure helps them learn more effectively by encountering various scenarios. The agents are modelled using Nomoto first-order dynamics, a standard model for ship manoeuvring. For training, the input state to the reinforcement learning (RL) network consists of a grid representing obstacle positions and angles relative to the agent, as well as the agent's own state information-such as heading error (HE), cross-track error (CTE), velocity (v), and rudder angle. The output of the RL model comprises the rudder angle rate and acceleration, which the agent uses to control its path and avoid obstacles in real time. A comprehensive reward function was developed, focusing on both target approach and obstacle avoidance, encouraging agents to minimize collisions while staying on course. A risk assessment model was developed to avoid unnecessary collision avoidance actions, which dynamically determines the switching time between path following and collision avoidance [4]. The system employs shared policy and critic networks, leading to faster training times and improved scalability, making it suitable for large, complex environments with many agents. Simulation results demonstrate that ASV s can successfully navigate environments with multiple dynamic obstacles, maintaining safe distances and following their intended paths. The system was rigorously tested in a custom simulation environment, built using the Ray, Stable Baselines3, Gymnasium, and other supporting Python libraries, offering a scalable and flexible platform for future maritime applications.

articleTitle: Robustness Analysis of Frequency-Difference Methods for Shallow-Water Source Localization Under Water Depth Mismatch
abstract: This study investigates the robustness of underwater source localization methods, specifically focusing on frequency-difference-based approaches: Matched Autoproduct Processing (MAP), Phase-Only Matched Autoproduct Processing (POMAP), and their cross-frequency coherent counterparts, CMAP and POCMAP. The research examines how these methods perform under varying water depth mismatch conditions. Through numerical simulations conducted in a shallow-water environment, the performance of these methods is systematically evaluated against the conventional Matched Field Processing (MFP). The results indicate that frequency-difference methods significantly outperform conventional MFP, resulting in lower localization errors in both range and depth. In particular, MAP and CMAP achieved a reduction in range root mean square error (RMSE) of approximately 70% relative to conventional MFP. Additionally, the frequency-difference methods achieved over a 56.9% success rate, while conventional MFP only demonstrated a 15.7% success rate when there was a 10% mismatch in water depth. These results demonstrate the potential of frequency-difference methods to provide more reliable source localization in scenarios with uncertain environmental parameters, thereby enhancing the robustness and practicality of underwater acoustic applications.

articleTitle: Robust Underwater Positioning System Using LED Markers and Perspective-n-Point Solver
abstract: Swarm operations of underwater robots are gaining attention as a means of performing more complex and efficient tasks underwater. For successful operation, each underwater robot must know its position and pose. Traditional underwater acoustic positioning using ultrasonic waves has the advantage of providing wide-area coverage. However, the large size of those systems makes them difficult to mount on smaller robots such as those used in underwater robot swarms. This paper proposes a new simultaneous position and pose measurement system suitable for underwater robot swarm operations. In this system, a camera is mounted on each robot, and the relative position and pose of the light-emitting diodes (LEDs) are based on the coordinates of several known LEDs and the images captured by the camera. The effectiveness of the proposed positioning system using LEDs and cameras is verified through experiments in a test tank.

articleTitle: Acoustic Multilateration for Marine Animal Tracking in Coral Reef Ecosystems: Combining Isodiachronic and Sequential Methods
abstract: This study introduces an enhanced acoustic mul-tilateration technique for marine animal localization that in-tegrates isodiachronic localization with sequential bound esti-mation methods, significantly improving positioning accuracy. The method improves localization reliability by systematically accounting for uncertainties in underwater sound speed, re-ceiver positions, and measurement errors. System performance was rigorously evaluated through extensive simulations using root mean square error (RMSE), bias, and standard deviation metrics. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves optimal positioning accuracy, particularly within the array coverage area, with a significant reduction in error using time-synchronized hydrophone arrays. Experimental validation using a five-hydrophone synchronized array will be conducted in the Keelung Chaojing Coral Reef Ecological Area to confirm the simulation results.

articleTitle: Uncertainties in River Flow Measurements Using Acoustic Tomography: Potentials and Challenges
abstract: Providing precise records of streamflow measurements, mainly during floods, is essential for understanding the evolution dynamics of river channels, projecting future flow records, and introducing best management plans. In some cases, conventional measurement methods fail to provide reliable estimates of streamflow data during unsteady flow conditions. Recently, underwater acoustics tomography-based methods have been considered as promising potential to provide accurate river flow measurements. The objective of this work is to investigate the potential of a new generation of acoustic tomographic system designed to overcome challenges associated with accurate river flow measurement in restricted river geometries. In particular, we aim to monitor accurate streamflow within a narrow and extremely shallow river. The utilized system employs acoustic signals to map the sound speed across the entire river cross-section, and thus enables accurate and continuous measurements of the cross-sectional average velocity and river flow. The findings showed that the utilized system can be operated within extremely shallow depths > 10 cm, Interestingly, the flow estimated by the FAT system was very comparable with other reference datasets obtained by additional independent methods, especially, during high flow conditions. However, the presence of high sediment particles generated during flood events weakened the quality of acoustic signals which resulted in measurement failures during these periods.

articleTitle: Underwater Sea Cucumber Detection Using Consumer-Grade Amphibious UAV and Deep-Learning Based Computer Vision
abstract: Holothurians (commonly known as sea cucumber) have economic and ecological value, as they are considered fishery resources, nutrient regulators, bioturbators, and indicator species in coral reef ecosystems. Therefore, continuous monitoring of Holothurians provides insights into ecosystem status and decision-making for ecological conservation and resource management. Traditional monitoring techniques are labor-intensive, constrained by the hardware, limited by obsolete algorithms, lack professional ecological information, and only cover a limited spatial scale. Based on a field survey conducted in Koh Tao, Thailand, a novel Holothurians monitoring system was established by combining a self-designed consumer-grade amphibious Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (AUAV) with a Mamba-based Super-Resolution Reconstruction (SRR) technique and an enhanced YOLOv10 instance segmentation model. Super-resolution (SR) images reconstructed by the MambaIR model were input into the proposed YOLOv10 SEA model for instance segmentation of Holothurians. Habitat maps and demographic parameters were measured based on the output segmented map. The results show that the proposed system can monitor Holothurians efficiently and accurately, providing useful ecological information to conservation communities and decision-makers.

articleTitle: Evaluation of the Water Entry Impact of an Air-Launched AUV
abstract: Air-Launched Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AL-AUVS), deployable from an aircraft, provide a new operational alternative to traditional ship-based AUV transport and deployment. This study explores gliding AL-AUVs, that reduce impact forces upon water entry through aerodynamic wings. Experimental investigations using scaled AUV models demonstrated that the impact acceleration applied to the vehicle, when entering the water at terminal velocity without wings, remains within a safe range. Furthermore, the experimental conditions were successfully replicated using a particle based method, where the magnitude of the first acceleration peak closely matched the experimental results.

articleTitle: Tsunami Waves Detected by a Seafloor Fiber Optic Strainmeter
abstract: The Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC) has started continuous observations of crustal deformation using a fiber optic interferometry-based strainmeter in the Nankai Trough since 2019. In this study, we present the detection of tsunami waves caused by earthquakes that occurred off Torishima Island in 2023 and 2024 using optical fiber strainmeters. The amplitude of the strain associated with the 2023 tsunami was <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.003 \mathbf{\mu}\mathbf{\varepsilon}$</tex> ‘ On the other hand, the amplitude of the strain associated with the 2024 tsunami was <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.03 \mathbf{\mu}\mathbf{\varepsilon}$</tex>. This suggests that tsunami observations using fiber optic strainmeters can contribute to the early detection of non-seismogenic tsunamis offshore where there are few tsunami surveillance facilities.

articleTitle: Very Low Frequency Complex Dielectric Constant Measurement of Seawater for Underwater Electromagnetic Applications
abstract: A navigation system using low-frequency electromagnetic waves is being developed for the operation of robots under sea ice in the polar regions. The complex permittivity of seawater and sea ice is necessary to model the propagation characteristics of electromagnetic waves in the three layers: sea, sea ice and air. However, in the low frequency range, an electric double layer forms on the surface of the electrodes used for measurement and most of the capacitance to be measured is an electric double layer capacitor. To remove this capacitance and measure the complex permittivity of seawater itself, a method using the difference of impedances measured at two different electrode spacings is proposed and the measurement results are discussed. At present there are some cases where the difference can give a relative permittivity close to the theoretical value, but in most cases there is a large error in the measured value. In this paper the error factors are discussed and a modified proposed method to reduce the measurement error is reported.

articleTitle: Underwater Frequency Selection Algorithm Based on the Received Signal
abstract: Underwater communication is widely regarded as one of the most significant challenges due to the unique physical properties of water. Among the available communication methods, radiofrequency communication offers higher data transmission rates than acoustic communication. However, higher frequencies suffer from substantial attenuation in water, making it difficult to achieve long-distance transmission. Addressing the tradeoff between transmission rate and communication distance is essential for achieving optimal performance. Unlike conventional systems that rely on fixed operating frequencies, this study introduces a dynamic frequency selection algorithm. This algorithm dynamically adjusts the operating frequency in real-time based on channel conditions and transmission rate feedback, ensuring a more adaptive and efficient communication system. To validate this approach, a dipole antenna with multiple impedance matching was designed and tested in a water tank environment. The experimental results revealed that bandwidth performance varied across different frequencies. Transmission rate analysis showed that higher frequencies provided higher data transmission over short distances. Conversely, lower frequencies exhibited better signal stability and reliability for long-distance communication due to their reduced attenuation. These findings highlight the importance of adaptive frequency selection in underwater radiofrequency communication, where a balance between transmission rate and communication distance must be achieved to support various operational requirements.

articleTitle: Real-Time Distance Measurement Between Structures in Breakwater Construction Using a Multipath-Resistant Underwater Acoustic Positioning System
abstract: In this paper, we report on the installation of a multipath-resistant underwater acoustic positioning system developed by our team for real-time distance measurement between structures at breakwater construction sites. Experimental results from both a controlled testing pool and an actual construction site demonstrate that the system can achieve precise positioning with submeter-level accuracy. The successful application of this technology in construction projects highlights its potential to enhance the mechanized construction of underwater structures, such as breakwaters.

articleTitle: Improved Identification Evaluation of Side-Scan Sonar for Blue Carbon
abstract: Sonar can only provide information about the presence of objects at a given location. Therefore, the evaluation accuracy of sonar is lower than that of cameras and is not often used for identification of living organisms. The objective of this research is to improve the evaluation system by using sonar to identify the differences among amamo and sasabamo, which are surveyed as blue carbon, and waterweeds that are not surveyed, including ebimo, respectively. Sonar data were acquired by boat or on foot. The acquired data is Fourier transformed using MATLAB. The difference between the Fourier transformed images at each location is detected. The detected results are compared with the images taken by the underwater drone that was operated together with the survey to improve the accuracy. It is difficult to detect plants using only sonar data showing acoustic reflection intensity and underwater drone footage captured in turbid water with overexposure. Fourier transforms were performed for areas where plants were inhabited and areas where plants were not inhabited. The comparison of the two results revealed findings suggesting that differences can be observed even in areas with similar seabed conditions.

articleTitle: Towards an Autonomous Sampling System for the Hadal Zone
abstract: We present a vehicle system combining a small autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) with an underwater lander for use in an autonomous sampling system for hadal zone (depth of more than 6,000m) applications. When developing an ultra-deep sea vehicle system, the long vertical movement, the increased weight and size to withstand high water pressure or special equipment for hadal, the limitations of commercially available sensors, and underwater communication represent high barriers. We aim to overcome these challenges by sharing functions effectively between the AUV and the lander. The lander can be equipped with adequate flotation to move vertically, with large-capacity batteries and acoustic communication devices to support vessels, all of which can contribute to reduce the AUV weight, and offer good maneuverability and payload for sampling capabilities despite the hadal applications. We also assume that acoustic positioning of the AUV from the lander provides a solution to sensor-limited AUV navigation. In addition to describing the concept, this paper presents preliminary experiments conducted using a prototype AUV for vehicle navigation assisted by acoustic positioning from a lander, and visual feed-back control assuming docking to the lander. These results support the benefits and feasibility of this concept and clarify future works to produce an autonomous sampling system.

articleTitle: In-Situ Monitoring of Nearshore Ocean Currents with Distributed Acoustic Sensing on a Submarine Cable
abstract: Nearshore ocean currents exhibit intricate complexities due to interactions among tides, rivers, and coastlines, making accurate modeling challenging. High-resolution, continuous in situ observations are essential for understanding these dynamics. In this study, we employed a 25-km-long submarine dark fiberoptic cable with distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) technology to record continuous signals associated with ocean waves. This innovative approach allows for real-time, high-resolution monitoring of underwater dynamics, which traditional methods may not capture with such detail or over such extensive areas. The use of DAS technology in oceanography is relatively new but promising due to its ability to convert each segment of the optical fiber into a series of individual receivers. This setup enables the detection of acoustic and seismic activities along the cable's entire length. In our deployment, part of the fiber-optic cable was installed inland and part extended underwater across the continental shelf, providing a unique cross-section of environmental interactions. The recorded signals demonstrate clear transition patterns between land and ocean, aligning well with tidal signals, suggesting the potential of this method for studying coastal interfaces. Microseismic noise induced by ocean surface gravity waves (OSGWs) was clearly observed in the 0.08–0.4 Hz frequency band for the submarine fiber segments. Interestingly, this signal was absent in the land fiber segments, highlighting the method's sensitivity to aquaticspecific phenomena. This distinction is critical for isolating marine signals from terrestrial noise, thereby improving the accuracy of data interpretation. We derived current velocity and water depth from velocity dispersion using frequency–wave number analysis matched against theoretical ocean wave propagation equations. This analysis involved comparing our measured data with models that predict how wave characteristics such as speed and frequency change with water depth and current flow. The method proved effective, as our results aligned closely with nearby current measurements and observations from a nearby tide gauge. These correlations underscore the reliability of DAS technology in capturing and quantifying dynamic oceanographic processes. These findings are significant, as they validate the feasibility of using DASinstrumented cables for real-time monitoring of nearshore ocean currents. The implications for this are broad and highly beneficial for coastal management. Accurate, real-time data on nearshore currents can enhance maritime safety, improve pollution tracking, and offer valuable insights for coastal development planning. Furthermore, the ability to monitor changes in current patterns over time can contribute to climate change research, particularly in understanding how rising sea levels and changing weather patterns, for instance typhoon, affect coastal and submarine environments. Moreover, the successful integration of DAS technology with existing oceanographic measurement tools could revolutionize how researchers study marine environments. By providing a detailed, continuous picture of underwater dynamics, DAS-equipped cables could significantly expand our understanding of underexplored or inaccessible areas of the ocean. Future research could explore the integration of this technology with satellite and drone observations to develop a comprehensive, multi-layered view of oceanic and coastal phenomena, enhancing our ability to protect and manage these vital ecosystems more effectively.

articleTitle: Underwater Acoustic Positioning Simulation and Sea Area Verification
abstract: This study investigates underwater acoustic propagation and localization in the southwestern waters of Taiwan, aiming to enhance maritime safety and vessel tracking capabilities. Utilizing a combination of numerical modeling and field experiments, the research examined sound transmission characteristics, optimized acoustic sensor placement, and evaluated the effectiveness of localization algorithms. Numerical simulations employing the Bellhop model [1] revealed efficient sound propagation patterns, guiding the design of field experiments. Field experiments involving both stationary and towed acoustic systems demonstrated accurate vessel localization within a 2 km radius, achieving horizontal errors below 100 m and depth errors less than 2 m. These findings highlight the feasibility of passive acoustic systems as a reliable and cost-effective supplement to traditional tracking methods such as AIS, effectively addressing limitations in maritime surveillance. The study establishes a robust framework for integrating advanced acoustic technologies into maritime security strategies, providing valuable insights for real-time monitoring and environmental adaptability in challenging underwater conditions. Future applications include expanding operational ranges and enhancing data processing capabilities for broader use in marine resource management and national defense.

articleTitle: Sensorics of Marine Digital Holographic Bioindication Station
abstract: The paper presents a bioindication complex - DHC-FOCL probe - used to monitor and build the time series of autochthonous plankton concentrations based on underwater digital holography. It also shows the results of field digital holographic experiments in various water areas on the interpretation of data characterizing the behavioral activity of plankton in the habitat.

articleTitle: Experimental Examination of Preloading for Strainmeters in Deep Seafloor Boreholes
abstract: Geodetic and seismic observation in deep seafloor boreholes can monitor activities around subducting plates with higher precisions relative to other observations taking advantage of shorter distances to plate boundaries and lower noise levels. One of the key techniques to provide precise observation is to couple the sensor to the surrounding media. This study examines the coupling condition of a sensor of a strainmeter in the borehole through a laboratory experiment. The sensor was cemented in a tank that simulates a borehole. Strain and temperature variations were recorded continuously until 30 days after the beginning of the cementing experiment. Since the strain records contained large amplitude of thermal responses, reduction of them by a model fitting was performed. After the reduction, preloading condition was suggested from a strain variation of extension of the sensor with time.

articleTitle: Investigation Method for Identifying the Distribution of Freshwater Blue Carbon
abstract: In this study, we will examine the survey methods for freshwater blue carbon, which is thought to be a carbon sink rather than a source of carbon dioxide emissions. The freshwater blue carbon that is attracting attention is the Japanese endemic species Sasa Vamos, and we will use CycleGAN to clarify images and side scan sonar and multi-beam sonar to confirm whether it is possible to acquire features that can be used to distinguish whether or not this species is growing in the water or near the water surface. Data acquisition was carried out at a reservoir in Kobe City and Lake Biwa.

articleTitle: A Preliminary Study of Forward-Looking Sonar Based Path Planning for Remotely Operated Vehicles
abstract: Unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) are broadly categorized into remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) and autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), each offering unique advantages. These vehicles are widely used in scientific research, engineering, civilian applications, and national defense. Underwater missions often encounter diverse environmental conditions and objectives, with UUVs equipped with distinct instrument configurations and motion characteristics. Consequently, path planning becomes a critical factor directly tied to mission requirements, significantly influencing UUV performance. Evaluating whether a planned path meets mission demands or selecting the most suitable path from multiple options is vital for enhancing the success rate of UUV operations. This paper focuses on using an ROV equipped with a multi-beam forward-looking sonar to conduct a comprehensive scan of a designated three-dimensional (3D) water area within a limited timeframe. To achieve this, multiple path planning methods were developed to ensure complete scanning coverage of cylindrical water volumes. These methods leverage the sonar's measurement range, horizontal beam width, vertical beam width, and the defined water area. Each path planning output consists of planar scanning paths at varying depths. By calculating the total scanning path length and diving depth, combined with the ROV speed specifications, the total time required to complete the scanning mission is estimated.

articleTitle: Bio-Inspired Surfaces for Turbulence Reduction
abstract: While the topic of bio-inspired flow control has been an area of active study since early in the last century, there has been renewed interest in recent years in both passive (shark skin) and active (dolphin skin) methods of flow control to reduce hydrodynamic drag and boundary layer turbulence. This renewed interest is mainly due to advances in technology, in particular additive manufacturing, soft robotics, and micro-electronics. In this work, we investigate the impact of shark skin denticle surfaces, as well as actively modulated boundaries with and without added roughness elements, on near-boundary velocity to improve our understanding of the underlying mechanism and work towards implementation in underwater platforms. We developed a set of shark-skin inspired denticle inserts and soft membranes using advanced additive manufacturing techniques and characterized the impact on the velocity field in a flow channel under varying flow conditions. Accompanying high-order numerical simulations show a change in vorticity over the denticle-covered surface, in a pattern consistent with laboratory experiments. The respective changes to the velocity profile provide guidance for implementation of boundary layer control methods (active and passive) on in-water vehicles.

articleTitle: Seismicity Observation at Hyuga-Nada Subduction Zone by Ocean Bottom Seismometer from 2015 to 2024
abstract: The Nankai Trough, extending from Suruga Bay to offshore Kyushu, marks the subduction boundary where the Philippine Sea Plate descends beneath the Eurasian Plate. This region is seismically active, with Hyuga-nada experiencing a magnitude 7.1 earthquake in August 2024, though no historical record exists of magnitude greater than 8 events there. Slow earthquakes, including low-frequency tremors and very low-frequency earthquakes (VLFEs), frequently occur at the plate boundary. Marine seismic networks deployed from 2015 to 2024 in Hyuga-nada used Long-Term Ocean Bottom Seismometers (LT-OBS) to monitor seismic activity. Precise event relocations combined 1D and 3D velocity structures, using double-difference seismic tomography method and then determine the first-motion focal mechanisms to refine hypocenters and classify earthquake mechanisms. Results show seismicity concentrated at depths of 14–20 km, with diverse focal mechanisms dominated by strike-slip and normal fault types. Most earthquakes likely originate within the subducting Philippine Sea Plate rather than the plate boundary. Additionally, the spatial-temporal distribution of swarm events of regular earthquakes and VLFEs suggests that their seismicity may be related, with VLFEs potentially triggering subsequent regular earthquakes.

Author Keywords: seismicity in a subducting oceanic plate

articleTitle: Study of Accuracy Improvement of UAV-Based Seafloor Crustal Deformation Observation
abstract: As a countermeasure against the risk of large earthquakes, the GNSS-A observation is being used to observe seafloor crustal deformation. However, it is difficult to improve the frequency and immediacy of the observation due to its high cost and physical limitations of the low-speed platforms. In this study, a GNSS-A observation system using a seaplane-type UAV (HAMADORI 6000) was developed and demonstrated. The reliability of the acoustic ranging was evaluated in the tank test, and we successfully determined the seafloor position with high accuracy the first time in a sea trial. However, it was failed to make an observation the second time due to system trouble. Robustness of the system is an issue for the future.

articleTitle: Dynamic Geometry Fitting for Probabilistic Localization of Auv for Mooring Line Inspection
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of improving Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) self-localization, providing precise navigation for Floating Offshore Wind Turbine (FOWT) mooring line inspections. Building on previous works proposing a mooring line tracking method for AUVs, we employ a particle filter algorithm that integrates geometry fitting for detected mooring lines with dead-reckoning data, without requiring additional acoustic positioning systems. The method was validated through simulation experiments for both catenary and taut mooring line scenarios under various sensor measurement error conditions. Results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves AUV localization and mooring line estimation performance compared to dead-reckoning alone and is expected to provide a robust solution for inspecting underwater structures.

articleTitle: An Underwater Self-Positioning System with a Smartphone Based on Visual-Inertial Odometry and Trajectory Matching
abstract: The introduction of net cleaning robots is required in aquaculture. For an efficient operation of net cleaning robots, a high-precision underwater self-positioning system is required. In this research, we have proposed and verified a method by VIO and trajectory matching using a smartphone for the purpose of implementing a small underwater self-positioning system to be implemented in a net cleaning robot. The verification results shows that the system is possible to achieve highly accurate self-position estimation by correcting the estimated position by trajectory matching.

articleTitle: Coastal Soundscape Around Japan
abstract: The coastal waters around Japan are highly diverse, supporting a range of tropical, warm, and cold-water species. During the winter, strong monsoons sweep across Japan from west to east, creating a stark contrast between the sea conditions on the Japan Sea side and the Pacific Ocean side. To understand coastal soundscape, we monitored underwater sounds at 10 coastal sites around Japan to collect baseline data for the environmental assessment of potential offshore wind farm projects. Obtained data highlight regional and seasonal differences.

articleTitle: The Concentration of Particulate Organic Carbon Investigation Using One-Dimensional Vertical Computational Fluid Dynamic Coupling Biochemical Model
abstract: As the largest carbon sink, the ocean plays a crucial role in achieving carbon neutrality. Phytoplankton, which thrive in the euphotic zone, drive primary productivity by providing energy for marine ecosystems and serving as a vital component of marine carbon storage. Among the acquisition methods of oceanographic data, in situ observations, remote sensing, and numerical models, the data from in situ observation is valuable but limited. Remote sensing provides rapid, wide-range imagery, however, lacking information on subsurface distributions. The numerical models involve numerous parameters but vary depending on the specific region. To facilitate easier estimation of particulate organic carbon (POC) concentrations across the region surrounding Taiwan, we revised and simplified the one-dimensional vertical model proposed by Omstedt [1]. By omitting time evolution effects and seabed terrain distribution, the major input parameters for the current model are reduced to sea surface temperature and wind speed. The results from this numerical model show qualitative trends and scales comparable to those of in situ measurements. Additionally, to leverage the strengths of both remote sensing and numerical modeling, we present a mixing model that combines results from both approaches. Comparisons of euphotic zone depth between in situ measurements and estimates from various methods (remote sensing, numerical model, and mixing model) suggest that the mixing model offers potential for improved POC estimation accuracy.

articleTitle: Design a Drift Path for Unmanned Surface Vehicles using Nonlinear Model Predictive Control
abstract: With the advancement of unmanned driving technology, Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USVs) have become a significant topic in marine exploration, environmental monitoring, and military applications. USVs are characterized by their efficiency, flexibility, and remote-control capabilities, playing an increasingly important role in surface operations. As the number of USVs increases, the issues of automated charging, maintenance, and management will become substantial time and labor resource burdens. However, the automatic docking of USVs faces numerous technical challenges. Due to the differences in driving mechanisms, inertia, and resistance between vessels and vehicles, the kinematic principles applicable to vehicles are not suitable for small boats, making it impossible to employ parallel parking methods used for vehicles directly. Consequently, using drift docking technology for USVs has emerged as a critically important solution, enabling fully automated management of unmanned fleets, including automatic cruising, docking, and charging, thereby reducing labor and time-related maintenance costs. This paper uses nonlinear model predictive control and the Gazebo platform as the algorithm and simulation environment for USV drift parking. A dual-propeller USV controller is designed using a simplified kinematic-dynamic bicycle model. The simulation results show that this method can successfully operate on the Gazebo platform and has the possibility of being implemented in an environment where unmanned ships sail in real waters.

articleTitle: Study on Course Design of Cruising AUV for Docking at Deep-Sea Terminal
abstract: Underwater docking technology has gained attention as a means to extend the operating time and survey range of Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs). In docking operations, the cruising AUVs cannot hover and stand by at a fixed point. Therefore, they must be able to perform a retry operation, that is, disengage and approach again. Although retrying over short distances has the advantage of saving time, it has the disadvantage of reducing the straight-line stability. In this case, the setting of the course design must be identified. This paper focused on the waypoint navigation of a cruising AUV and determines the setting of shortest course design to stabilize the AUV just before docking by numerical simulation. Moreover, this study demonstrates the procedure of the planning course design for docking of cruising AUV.

articleTitle: Recognition and Classification of Ship Noise in Underwater Soundscape Based on Yet Another Mobile Network and Unmanned Surface Vehicle
abstract: This paper proposes using Yet another mobile network (YAMNet) to detect engine noise from ships within the underwater soundscape. This novel approach combines deep learning with sound classification techniques to accurately identify and categorize engine noises from various vessels in the marine environment. It holds significant potential for marine ecological protection, ship management, and noise pollution control applications. YAMNet is a deep learning model based on the MobileNet architecture, designed for audio event detection and classification. MobileNet is a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) known for its high computational efficiency and compactness, making it suitable for execution on resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) devices through edge computing. YAMNet was originally designed to effectively process audio data from various environments by converting sound signals into spectrograms, which are then processed through the deep learning network for feature extraction and classification. This enables YAMNet to quickly and accurately recognize various audio events, such as natural sounds, mechanical noises, and human activities.

articleTitle: A Novel Approach to Estimate Three-Dimensional Current Fields Using Coastal Acoustic Tomography System in the Yeosu Bay, South Korea
abstract: Coastal acoustic tomography (CAT) is a technology used to monitor changes in current or water temperature fields by analyzing reciprocal acoustic travel time signals between CAT stations in coastal seas. We have developed a novel method for estimating three-dimensional current fields by combining an inverse method with an artificial intelligence (AI) model. To test the newly-developed method, we first ran the ray tracing model ‘Bellhop’ to compute reciprocal travel times among five CAT stations using high-resolution ocean model outputs. These five stations correspond to the locations where in-situ CAT systems were established for continuous monitoring of current changes in the Yeosu Bay, South Korea. Subsequently, the range-averaged currents at the five layers were estimated by incorporating the travel time difference data into an AI model trained with the same ocean model outputs. Finally, the inverse method was applied to each layer to estimate the 3-D current fields. Validation results revealed that this method performed reasonably well, producing time-varying two-layer-like current fields in the study area. They occasionally revealed an out-of-phase relationship between the upper and lower layers depending on the tidal phases. This method yielded average RMSEs of less than 5 cm/s on six simulation paths. These results indicate that our method can be effectively applied to 3-D current field monitoring in coastal seas using a CAT system.

articleTitle: FEM-Based Study of Acoustic Shadowing Effects on Underwater Acoustic Vector Sensor Due to Nearby Supports
abstract: For passive measurements of acoustic signals for oceanographic and military applications, an Acoustic Vector Sensor (AVS) may be used. A PU AVS is a compact sensor that measures a four-dimensional vector quantity of acoustic particle velocity in the water medium along three orthogonal axes and scalar pressure. Its primary purpose is to sense these four components from which the acoustic intensity vector is derived to estimate the Direction of Arrival (DOA) of one or more radiating acoustic sources in the medium. This sensor is deployed in water with the help of a supporting structure of a mother platform. Also, the AVS assembly may be placed inside a protective cage. However, these structures might act as potential obstacles to the propagation of sound waves, thereby corrupting the signals being captured by the AVS and thus reducing the accuracy of the DOA estimation. Understanding these effects is crucial for optimizing the deployment and operation of AVS systems in real-world scenarios. To estimate the impact of acoustic shadowing, we conduct Finite Element Method (FEM) simulations in COMSOL Multiphysics software and validate the findings experimentally. These analyses aid in strategically placing structures alongside the AVS during deployment, ultimately enhancing the accuracy of DOA estimates obtained from the recorded signals.

articleTitle: Performance Evaluation of the Low-Cost Virtual Reality System for Real-Time Visualization of Underwater Environments
abstract: Underwater operations involve many dangers. Recently, the use of robots has been progressed to improve safety. In such situations, it is important to have a means to better understand the robot's situation. However, to put it to practical use, it is necessary not only to improve performance but also to consider cost. This paper proposes a low-cost system that enables real-time underwater video acquisition using a 360°camera and a head-mounted display (HMD), and evaluates whether the performance is sufficient for practical use. In this system, a 360° camera is mounted on the robot within communication range, and real-time images are transmitted to the HMD via a host computer. Experiments were conducted using actual equipment, both in the tank and at sea. The system was also evaluated based on the delay and image quality during these experiments. The delay depends on the amount of data in the packets sent to the HMD in a single communication. Therefore, experiments were conducted for each combination of several data sizes and two HMDs with different performance. As for image quality, a weight was placed in the tank and the visibility of the two HMDs at different distances was compared. Based on these experiments, it was found that this system can be operated with a level of delay that is acceptable for use and that the image quality, which leads to ease of use, depends only on the resolution of the camera.

articleTitle: Design and Offshore Tests of Multipurpose Deep-Sea Lander
abstract: Deep-sea landers are critical platforms for benthic ecosystem monitoring, environmental sampling, and in-situ data acquisition in the deep ocean. This study presents the development and implementation of an innovative deep-sea lander system, which was engineered by the Taiwan Ocean Research Institute of the National Applied Research Laboratories (TORI NARLabs). The platform features an aluminum alloy framework integrated with syntactic foam buoyancy elements, offering multiple modular mounting points and a payload capacity of 1000kg to support diverse scientific instrumentation. A distinctive twin-body configuration was specifically engineered to address the challenges posed by Taiwan's predominantly muddy seafloor, effectively preventing substrate adhesion and platform subsidence. Field validation trials successfully demonstrated the lander's operational effectiveness by collecting chemical parameters, biological samples, and photographic documentation, confirming its viability for deep-sea research applications.

articleTitle: Automatic High-Frequency Click Detection Algorithm for Cetaceans
abstract: The expansion of offshore wind power facilities in Taiwan's western waters poses significant threats to marine cetaceans, particularly the finless porpoise (Neophocaena phocaenoides sunameri), which is the most frequently stranded cetacean in the region. Causes of stranding include fishery bycatch, environmental changes, vessel collisions, and marine engineering activities. Traditional visual surveys are ineffective for monitoring this species due to its lack of a prominent dorsal fin, limiting the collection of ecological data and the development of conservation strategies. To overcome these challenges, we developed an automated detection algorithm for high-frequency (HF) cetacean clicks using underwater passive acoustic monitoring (PAM). The first algorithm utilized a time-domain computational approach, applying a high-pass filter (>110 kHz) and a peak detection algorithm to identify click trains, incorporating the Peak Energy Algorithm (Step A). The second algorithm introduced a band-pass filter (60–192 kHz) and combined Step A with a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) calculation (Step B). Additionally, two filters were integrated into the algorithm, informed by studies conducted in the Bohai Sea, Zhangzhou, and Hainan, China, to refine click event detection. Analysis of 7.5 hours of acoustic data from the Yun-Chang Rise validated the algorithm. The first algorithm achieved a precision ratio (PR) of 78.09% and a false positive ratio (FPR) of 8.06%, with misclassifications attributed to broadband pulses or closely spaced clicks. The second algorithm, incorporating the SNR threshold, improved PR to 96.3% (+17.4%) and reduced FPR to 0.89% (−7.17%). This algorithm enables efficient HF cetacean click detection and can be integrated into firmware for real-time marine operations. It provides a promising solution to the limitations of visual surveys, enhancing acoustic pattern recognition, and supporting improved cetacean monitoring and conservation in Taiwan's waters.

articleTitle: Formation Control Method of Multiple Autonomous Underwater Vehicles for Improving State Estimation Accuracy
abstract: This study proposes a method where multiple au-tonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) maintain the formation using relative positioning information obtained through acoustic positioning and communication to achieve stable state estimation. Underwater exploration by multiple AUVs is a useful method because environmental information can be obtained at multiple points simultaneously. However, when AUVs equipped with low-performance sensors are employed, their performance cannot be maintained independently, so a method is necessary to enable them to navigate correctly. This study developed a method to generate control commands to maintain formation based on angle and distance information obtained from acoustic positioning and communication between multiple AUVs, as well as their relative positions to surrounding AUVs. Simulations of autonomous navigation by multiple AUVs were conducted, and it was shown that the proposed method enables AUVs to perform stable state estimation while maintaining formation through the simulations.

articleTitle: Monitoring of Crustal Activity and Tsunami for Disaster Resilience from Oceanfloor Network System
abstract: In Japan, occurrence of future huge earthquakes is one of issues to be prepared, and Nankai trough earthquake is its candidate. In particular, Japan Meteorological Agency presents special information about the Nankai trough earthquake if activities around the Nankai trough area are observed. The local governments and the residents along the Nankai trough area stand ready for the occurrence. We regard that they have to prepare their issues considering the local characters of the disaster prevention. Here, we propose how to stand for it and it is monitoring crustal activities and tsunami using ocean-floor observation network system for earthquakes and tsunamis. In addition, risks of the earthquakes and tsunamis is also introduced on the mapping for the monitoring. Then, we carried out training for sending appropriate instructions for fields from the disaster headquarter using the monitoring system.

articleTitle: Distributed Acoustic Sensing Observation Using Seafloor Cable Observation System in the Japan Sea
abstract: In 2010, seafloor cabled observation system with a total length of 25 km and 4 stations was installed near Awashima island in the Japan Sea. A single armored optical fiber cable were buried 1 m below the seafloor to avoid a conflict with fishing activity, and has 8 optical fibers. One fiber pair for data transmission reaches the furthest station without repeater. Recently Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) is available for seismic observation. Spatially high-density data can be obtained for a long distance using DAS. Therefore, seismic observation using DAS technology on seafloor becomes popular at the present. We start observations of a DAS measurement from April 2023 using a fiber of the cable observation system in the Japan Sea. For the DAS measurement using the Japan Sea seafloor observation system, a fiber connecting the furthest station without repeater is used. An interrogator for the DAS measurement was installed in the landing station temporarily. The first observation was performed in April 2023 for approximately four days. As a result, micro-earthquakes occurring near the cable system was recorded, and we confirmed a good quality of DAS data. In September 2023, a DAS observation for about one-day was also carried out as a system evaluation after exchange of optical connectors in the landing station. The parameters of recording for the observation were identical to those for the first observation. We evaluated performance of DAS data from the first and second observations. The 2024 Noto-Hanto earthquake occurred on January 1st and many aftershocks followed. To record aftershocks, we made a DAS observation using the cable observation system in the Japan Sea from early February to late June, 2024. For aftershock observation, we used two sets of recording parameters for different recording periods. Reflecting an environment of the DAS observation, many aftershocks were recorded by the DAS observation.

articleTitle: Fundamental Researches on Advanced Sensing Technologies Using Laser Reflection in the Deep-Sea and on the Deep-Seabed
abstract: In order to establish the basis of new exploration method for seabed resource areas, we are currently focusing on the characteristics of laser reflection in the deep-sea and on the deep-seabed. And we are now working on fundamental researches on three different advanced sensing technologies using laser reflection from seabed and seawater, and aiming to establish the basis of elemental technologies that will contribute to seabed resource exploration. Now, to obtain the basic data required for these technologies and to verify the feasibility and practicality of them, three types of demonstrators for deep-sea use have been developing. They will be mounted on an actual underwater vehicle and used for evaluation tests in deep-sea areas. Evaluation tests for them have been conducted in a water-tank, shallow-water areas and deep-sea areas, and their basic performance desired as almost designed performance has been confirmed.

articleTitle: A Method of Avoiding Floating Obstacles During AUV Surfacing Using Sonar and Camera
abstract: Ice floes in polar regions make it difficult for Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) to surface safely after missions. In this paper, we propose a method to find safe areas for AUVs to surface by using camera images and scanning sonar data. Although this paper assumes operations of AUVs in polar regions where there are ice floes, the proposed method can be applied to other drifting obstacles. The underwater space is divided into three-dimensional grids, and the grids in which the ice floe exists are probabilistically estimated by a binary Bayes filter. To detect ice floes, we use a scanning sonar mounted on the AUV and a camera on the mother ship. The velocity of the ice floe is estimated from the camera images. Then, using a transition matrix that considers the velocity vector of the ice floe, the future obstacle occupancy probability 3D grid map (3D OOP Map) is predicted. Finally, considering the AUV's travel time, safe surfacing areas are shown on the obstacle occupancy probability 2D grid map (2D OOP Map). The method is verified through a tank experiment.

articleTitle: Application of Qualitative Research to Analyze the Knowledge and Skill Requirements for Maritime Operational Safety
abstract: Taiwan's geographical location is favorable, with its land surrounded by the sea, which provides natural advantages for the development of the marine industry. To promote the development of the marine industry while ensuring the sustainability of the marine environment, the Taiwanese government enacted the “Ocean Basic Act”[1] on November 1, 2019, outlining national policy guidelines for marine governance. This was followed by the release of the “National Ocean Policy White Paper”[2] in June 2020, and the passage of the “Marine Industry Development Act”[3] by the Legislative Yuan in May 2023. These policies represent significant steps in advancing marine affairs in Taiwan, guiding both central and local governments to work together to ensure sustainable marine development. The advancement of marine industries is closely related to the cultivation and development of marine talent. Today, while Taiwan is vigorously developing its marine industries, there are challenges such as (1) the disparity between marine talent cultivation and industry supply and demand, and (2) the misalignment between talent development and marine industry needs. Consequently, the next challenge in marine affairs will be the training of marine professionals. This study primarily aligns with the provisions related to the cultivation of professional talent specified in Article 10 and Article 11 of the “Marine Industry Development Act.” It aims to develop a core set of common competencies and curricula for marine industry talent. This will facilitate the smooth transition of our nation's industrial development model from a land-based perspective to a focus on marine areas, and gradually achieve the localization of marine industry professionals in our country. Considering the increasing number of individuals involved in marine operations and the complexity of interfaces, the knowledge and skills required for different marine operations and activities vary. “Safety” education is fundamental to implementing marine policies and promoting various marine industries. Although domestic safety training courses, such as the Global Wind Organization (GWO) basic safety training, have been introduced, there is still a lack of specialized training for marine operations safety. Moreover, a comprehensive competency-based safety course for marine operations has yet to be established. To address the need for different enterprises within the marine industry to ensure that marine professionals possess the ability to protect their own and their colleagues' safety while carrying out marine-related tasks, and to reflect the necessity of common safety competencies for these roles, this study employs qualitative research methods, utilizing purposive sampling to invite experts and practitioners from relevant marine fields to participate in “indepth interviews” and “focus group discussions. The research data identified the common core competency requirements for “marine operation safety” across different maritime job categories, resulting in eight major components, along with 23 items of “knowledge” and 26 items of “skills” corresponding to these competencies. It aims to integrate the common safety needs across different marine occupational categories, providing a scientific and evidence-based foundation for safety management within the marine industry. Additionally, the findings will serve as a reference for subsequent safety training programs for personnel in the marine industry.

articleTitle: Optimization of Pore Pressure Observation in a New Borehole Off the KII Channel: Toward High-Precision Extraction of Crustal Deformation Components
abstract: In January 2024, JAMSTEC operated real-time monitoring of pore pressure and fiber optical strain sensor in a new borehole off Kii Channel to monitor seismic activity and seafloor crustal deformation around the source region of Nankai earthquake. This paper will provide a brief review of our observatories along the Nankai Trough. Since the initial conditions have been reduced and the instrumental drift component has stabilized due to sufficient elapsed time, we will also present the crustal deformation extracted from the pore pressure data, discussing the influence of ocean disturbance as a noise factor and the stress impact on the seafloor pressure, which is thought to affect the generation cycle of slow slip events

articleTitle: Virtual Tethered Autonomous Underwater Vehicle with Communication Constraints
abstract: We propose that the two autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) be tethered with an optical link to share information through high-speed optical communication. In for-mation, AUVs need to share position information using acoustic ranging and communications for virtual tethering. To improve the utilization of the limited acoustic channel resources, we plan to differentiate the frequency at which each AUV performs acoustic ranging. We developed a reinforcement learning environment for acoustic ranging and communication decisions between multiple AUVs, and tested it in a simulated environment.

articleTitle: Evaluating the Potential Wave Energy Through Wave Spectrum Analysis: A Case Study on the North Coast of Taiwan
abstract: Taiwanese government addresses the goal of “net-zero carbon emissions by 2050,” it has recently focused on developing green energy. Due to its sustainability and abundance, marine energy has been particularly emphasized, especially wave energy. The solid northeast monsoons that blew to the northern coasts of Taiwan every winter provide ample wind and wave energy. However, the wave activity seems weak during summer except for Typhoon invasion periods. The predominant waves of typhoon-induced are swell, which poses potential damage risks to wave energy converters. This study selects Long Dong on the northern coast of Taiwan as the research area, with data from wave buoys set up by the Central Weather Administration. The results show that the wind wave energy during the monsoon period is greater than the non-monsoon period. There are several extreme surge wave energy during the non-monsoon period.

articleTitle: Multi-Feature Optimization and Recognition Method for Bionic Underwater Acoustic Communication Signals Mimicking Dolphin Whistles
abstract: In light of the shortcomings of existing methods for extracting the features of bionic UAC signals mimicking dolphin whistles, a multi-feature optimization and recognition method for bionic U AC signals is proposed. Firstly, the similar-ity between the two signals is qualitatively and quantitatively analyzed. Secondly, a multi-feature optimization method based on the NSGA-II optimization algorithm is proposed. Thirdly, an SVM classification model was constructed, and the accuracy of the proposed method was validated through a recognition test. And finally, a comparison was conducted between the per-formance before and after optimization, the proposed method has been demonstrated to result in a significant enhancement in the recognition rate.

articleTitle: The Real-Sea Anchor Testing of Floating Kuroshio Turbine off Xiaoliuqiu
abstract: The overuse of fossil fuels has led to the gradual depletion of energy resources, resulting in rising energy procurement costs and economic crises in many countries. Additionally, the heavy reliance on fossil fuel combustion has significantly contributed to global warming, causing more frequent natural disasters driven by climate change. This situation has created an urgent need for the global development of clean and renewable energy sources. The 2015 Paris Agreement set the goal of “limiting global temperature rise to well below 2°C above preindustrial levels, while pursuing efforts to restrict the increase to 1.5°C.” Furthermore, it aims for net-zero carbon emissions by 2050. As a result, countries around the world are increasingly prioritizing the development of renewable energy. Taiwan, an island with limited natural resources, relies on imports for more than 98% of its energy, significantly impacting its energy security. The majority of these imports are fossil fuels, such as coal and oil, which release large amounts of carbon dioxide when used, contributing to the greenhouse effect. In response to the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster following the Great East Japan Earthquake, the Taiwanese government reconsidered the country's energy supply security and gradually reduced the proportion of nuclear power in its energy mix, aiming to achieve a nuclear-free homeland by 2025. Given the twin goals of phasing out nuclear energy and achieving net-zero carbon emissions, the development of renewable energy has become a key policy objective. Among renewable energy sources, marine energy is an emerging field with significant potential due to its higher energy density compared to wind power. Marine energy involves converting the kinetic energy of moving water into electrical energy, including ocean current energy, thermal energy, tidal energy, and wave energy. Ocean current energy, in particular, is promising because ocean currents provide stable velocity and direction, making them a clean and reliable renewable energy source. Taiwan, surrounded by the ocean, benefits from the Kuroshio Current, which flows through its eastern waters. This current is part of the North Pacific Gyre, the second-largest ocean current in the world. The Kuroshio passes eastern Taiwan at a velocity of 1.0 to 1.5 m/s, with an energy potential of 20.7 to 22.1 Sv (10^{6} m^{3}/s) [1]. If properly harnessed, the Kuroshio Current could serve as a base-load power source. To meet the 2050 net-zero carbon goal, develop clean energy to reduce over-reliance on fossil fuels, and enhance energy self-sufficiency, Taiwan began research and development on Floating Kuroshio Turbine (FKT) systems in 2015, which is divided into two phases. The first phase, initiated in 2015 under the National Science Council's NEP-I and NEP-II projects, focused on the development of floating Kuroshio turbine systems, including simulation and design. This phase culminated in the successful completion of a 1:25 scale 800W floating Kuroshio turbine model, which was verified through towing channel tests in 2018. The second phase, led by the Ocean Affairs Council, began in 2019 and concentrated on scaling up the model to a 1:5 scale prototype and conducting field tests. In 2020, a 10kW prototype was developed and towing tested at sea, and in 2021, a 20kW floating Kuroshio turbine system was built and successfully tested for power generation during sea towing trials, This study conducted a 20kW system sea anchoring power generation test off the southwest coast of Xiaoliuqiu, Pingtung In 2022. The experimental results showed that with a flow velocity of 1 m/s, Generator 1 produced 3.72 kWh, while Generator 2 produced 3.38 kWh, resulting in a total output of 7.1 kWh, with an efficiency of 80%. These results demonstrate the feasibility of Kuroshio power generation, and the data will serve as a reference for the commercial design of the turbine system

articleTitle: Theoretical Model of Differential Acoustic Travel Times in a Deep Stratified Lake
abstract: We have been developing the lacustrine application of Coastal Acoustic Tomography (“CAT”) at Lake Biwa, Japan. We are targeting reliable measurement of ray path-averaged currents by differential travel time. As the largest lake in Japan, Biwa supplies water to 14 million; it has a mean depth in its main “Northern Basin” of 41 m and is stratified from May through December. This work theoretically models the “differential travel time” (DTT) between transducers deployed near the bottom of the lake, at ranges exceeding 5 km under stratified conditions. Notably, we investigate the importance of including the influence of current shear on the ray paths, an effect that is usually neglected when computing DTT. Our model is designed with reference to conditions from a field experiment in the North Basin of Lake Biwa, Japan, in November 2018, for which the thermocline lay at a depth of about 30 m. Deep water is taken to be motionless and to have a constant sound speed. Within the “internal reflection” zone at the thermocline, both current and sound speed are assumed to increase linearly upward, at rates typical of our field experiments. Under these assumptions, the rays are straight in the deep water, and circular in the thermocline. Accordingly, one can easily construct an eigenray from one bottom reflection to the next, with or without account for the effect of current shear on the paths of eigenrays, which allows us to evaluate this influence on computation of DTT.

articleTitle: Mooring Observations of Near-Inertial Waves in the Southern South China Sea
abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) “RAI” (C5) in December 2021, significantly enhance near-inertial waves (NIWs) in the southern South China Sea (SCS). Observations near Taiping Island from 2020–2022 show that RAI increased wave heights to 6 m, wind speeds to 20 m/s, and generated strong currents <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(> 0.5\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s})$</tex> in the upper 300 m. Wavelet analysis reveals intensified near-inertial frequencies (~66.6 hours) post-RAI, with near-inertial kinetic energy reaching 10–20 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{J}/\mathrm{m}^{3}$</tex> in open waters and 5–10 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{J}/\mathrm{m}^{3}$</tex> in shallow areas. The ADCP data highlights downward NIW propagation and strong current shear in the upper 100 m.

articleTitle: Ranging of Moving Sound Source Using Single Hydrophone in Shallow Waters
abstract: This study proposes an algorithm to estimate the radial velocity of a moving sound source as well as the distance to the source using acoustic data recorded on a single hydrophone. The proposed algorithm is based on the field differencing technique which measures the radial velocity of the sound source by cross-correlating the sound fields at different source-receiver ranges and estimates the range to the source by matching the measured radial velocity profile with the radial velocity model hypothesized by the range. Because the proposed algorithm considers the Doppler shift incurred by the source movement, it allows correct selection of the signal of interest and robust calculation of the cross-correlated field. The proposed algorithm is verified using the SWellEx-96 experiment data, and the data analysis results show that the proposed algorithm estimates the source track parameters at longer distances than the original form of the field differencing method.

articleTitle: Localization of AUVs Using Higher Order Sliding Mode Observer and Extended Kalman Filter
abstract: The localization of Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) is a challenging problem compared to the one of ground vehicles, given the impossibility of using Global Positioning System (GPS) in undersea environments. In this paper, we propose Higher Order Sliding Mode (HOSM) observer, compared to Extended Kalman Filter (EKF), for the self-localization of an AUV with acoustic positioning. Employing bearing, elevation and depth difference measurements with respect to a surface vessel, the designed observers are able to estimate the North and East positions and the heading of the underwater vehicle. Both the HOSM observer and the EKF are then integrated with a dynamic surface controller to address the trajectory tracking problem of the AUV. Simulations carried out in Matlab/Simulink compare the performances of the two approaches.

articleTitle: Investigation for Improvements in the Reconstruction of Tidal Currents by Coastal Acoustic Tomography with Data Assimilation
abstract: One of the factors affecting the performance of the numerical ocean model for coastal tidal currents is the open boundary conditions that drive the model interior. This study investigated the use of reciprocal acoustic transmission and resulting path-averaged currents to adjust the open boundary conditions. The boundary conditions were generated by utilizing state estimation results of sequential data assimilation with an ensemble Kalman filter scheme. Two modified open boundary conditions were evaluated: modifying the harmonic constants and directly using the time series of the EnKF results for the normal velocity. Both the two models with the new open boundary condition improved the agreement with the observed path-averaged currents. The model with the time series of the EnKF results partly reconstructed spike-like variation found in the observed path-averaged currents. Yet, high-frequency variation in the observed path-averaged currents cannot be reproduced in detail. Further consideration will be needed to improve the model so that it can reproduce the observed path-averaged currents including their high-frequency variation.

articleTitle: Dimensional Uncertainty Quantification for Laser-Scanning-Based Underwater 3D Reconstructions
abstract: High-resolution seafloor mapping from autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) or remotely operated vehicles is an important tool for assessing benthic ecosystems and infrastructure, which is increasingly becoming routine. While single surveys show a snapshot in time of the state of such environments, repeat surveys can identify how these change over time. To gauge whether changes are statistically significant, it is necessary to quantify the uncertainty of such 3D reconstructions; however, most 3D reconstruction methods do not provide any such measure. While there are various sources of uncertainty when reconstructing seafloor terrain data from structured light surveys, this research focusses on the contribution from the line laser pose uncertainty to the dimensional uncertainty of laser-scanning-based underwater 3D reconstructions. A Monte Carlobased approach is used to model the laser fan pose uncertainty from stereo images of the laser line projection acquired from various distances from the seafloor. The method is demonstrated on data acquired at the Southern Hydrate Ridge off the coast of Oregon with the SeaXerocks 3 mapping device deployed with the AE2000f AUV.

articleTitle: Application of Virtual Time-Reversal and Pulse Position Modulation for Underwater Acoustic Communication in Dynamic Shallow-Water Environments
abstract: The challenges of underwater acoustic communication in shallow water environments are dominated by severe multipath propagation and dynamic channel variations, resulting in intersymbol interference (ISI) and Doppler shifts from mobile platforms. This paper introduces an innovative communication architecture that combines three key techniques: pulse position modulation (PPM), multi-Doppler matched filtering, and virtual time-reversal (VTR). The system's cornerstone is a novel block-wise VTR approach that adaptively responds to channel variations while maintaining signal clarity. Initial system validation through water tank experiments demonstrated successful signal processing and hardware implementation under controlled conditions. The system's reliability was further verified through simulations incorporating real field environments and actual seafloor topography. Experimental results showed successful decoding of all test transmissions, while simulations confirmed robust performance under complex channel conditions. Field experiments are planned to evaluate system performance in dynamic ocean environments, where mobile platforms and varying oceanographic conditions present additional challenges. Our integrated approach presents a significant advancement in reliable underwater communication for complex nearshore environments, with potential applications in marine research, ocean exploration, and autonomous underwater vehicle operations.
