articleTitle: Application of Ambient Pressure-Driven Pumping Technology for Underwater pH Measurement
abstract: In this study, the power-free pumping technology utilizing ambient hydrostatic pressure in the underwater environment was applied to realize a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathbf{p H}$</tex> measurement system with an in situ calibration capability. A glass microfluidic pressure reducer was connected to a 3D-printed fluidic platform containing a pH sensor device for the evaluation of the flow-switching performance to supply <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathbf{p H}$</tex> standards and a seawater sample. As a result, the microfluidic pressure reducer and fluidic platform worked properly with unfiltered natural seawater sample.

articleTitle: Parameter Selection for Using Permutation Entropy in Cetacean Whistle Detection
abstract: This study investigates the optimal parameter selection for permutation entropy (PE) in cetacean whistle detection, focusing on the Indo-Pacific humpback dolphin (Sousa chinensis). PE, a statistical measure quantifying time series complexity, has shown promise in signal detection within noisy environments. However, its effectiveness heavily depends on two key parameters: embedding dimension <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(d)$</tex> and embedding delay <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\tau)$</tex>. Through systematic analysis of simulated tonal and broadband signals, we explore how different combinations of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$d$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau$</tex> affect detection performance, quantified by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta H$</tex> - the difference in PE between signal-plus-noise and noise-only sections. Our findings demon-strate that <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$d=6$</tex> offers an optimal balance between detection accuracy and computational efficiency. For <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau$</tex>, we establish a relationship with sampling frequency <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(f_{s})$</tex> and signal frequency <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(f_{0})$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau=f_{s}/(2f_{0})$</tex> maximizes <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta H$</tex>. This relationship allows for adaptive parameter selection across various cetacean species and recording conditions. We further validate our approach using simulated broadband signals that mimic the down-sweep characteristics of Indo-Pacific humpback dolphin whistles. This study provides a comprehensive framework for optimizing PE-based cetacean whistle detection, enhancing the sensitivity and reliability of acoustic monitoring techniques in marine mammal research and conservation efforts.

articleTitle: Inspection of Steel Sheet-Pile Quaywall Using Underwater Remotely Operated
abstract: Steel sheet pile wharves are integral to port infrastructure, necessitating routine inspections to ensure their structural safety and longevity. Traditional inspection methods, involving divers equipped with cameras, focus on visual assessments, thickness measurements, and cathodic protection system evaluations. While effective, these methods are labor-intensive and expose divers to significant risks. This work explores the use of a Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) as an alternative for inspecting two steel sheet pile wharves, labeled A and B. The ROV-based inspections were compared to conventional diver-based methods in terms of defect detection, biofouling removal efficiency, and steel thickness measurements. The findings reveal that ROV inspections offer several advantages, including enhanced safety, reduced operational time, and comparable accuracy in detecting structural anomalies. However, challenges such as limited visibility due to marine growth and calibration issues with thickness measurements were noted. This work proposes strategies to address these challenges, emphasizing the need for optimized ROV designs and improved operational protocols. By demonstrating the feasibility and benefits of ROV technology, this research provides valuable insights for advancing underwater inspection methods, ensuring safer and more efficient maintenance of steel sheet pile wharves.

articleTitle: Development of a Peristaltic Ice Drilling Robot for Arctic Under-Sea Ice Exploration -Evaluation of Excavation Performance of an Excavation Unit-
abstract: In this study, we developed an excavation unit for an ice drilling robot. This unit reduces contact between the excavated ice and the borehole wall, preventing ice refreezing. Additionally, a blade attached to the center of the drill tip effectively crushes ice at the borehole center. Experiments confirmed the transportation of excavated ice and the crushing of ice at the borehole center, demonstrating the effectiveness of reducing the exposed length of the auger and utilizing a central blade.

articleTitle: Real-Time Current Mapping Using Time-Reversal Coastal Acoustic Tomography: Theoretical Framework and Hardware Validation
abstract: This paper introduces a Time-Reversal Coastal Acoustic Tomography (TR-CAT) system designed for real-time mapping of coastal currents. Using time-reversal techniques, the system overcomes the limitations of traditional Ocean Acoustic Tomography (OAT), eliminating the need for reciprocal transmissions and instrument retrieval. This innovation simplifies the process of estimating differential travel times (DTTs), which are crucial for current measurements. The functionality of the TR-CAT system was validated through water tank experiments, which confirmed the accuracy of its hardware and signal processing methods in a controlled environment. Simulations showed strong alignment with theoretical predictions for DTT estimation, further demonstrating the system's reliability. Field experiments are planned to evaluate the system's performance in more complex ocean environments. The TR-CAT system represents a step forward in enhancing the efficiency of real-time ocean current monitoring.

articleTitle: Lifelong Clustering for Seafloor Images Interpretation in AUV Surveys
abstract: Online image interpretation to show habitat distribution patterns is essential for enhancing the environmental perception of Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs). Classifi-cation methods are challenging to perform because the collected images may fall outside predefined classification boundaries. Clustering, however, offers an alternative approach without relying on predefined boundaries. To enable online image interpre-tation, we propose a LifeLong Clustering (LLC) method, which incrementally clusters streaming data. Specifically, a memory bank is employed to store a sparse subset of previously collected images to reduce the computational load. Cluster merging and splitting techniques are utilized to maintain the model components adaptively, ensuring it accommodates new data while pre-serving previously learned knowledge. The clustering results on a field survey dataset demonstrate that the proposed LLC method achieves an average Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) score of 0.65 when compared to the Non-LLC method, and 0.62 when compared to other LLC results obtained from different survey paths. It highlights the robustness and reliability of the proposed method, showcasing its ability to deliver consistent clustering results across varying conditions. This consistency underscores the potential of the method to enhance AUV decision-making in real-time, enabling more informed and efficient operations.

articleTitle: Investigation of Differential Acoustic Travel Times (DTT) in a Stratified Lake at Superkilometer Ranges
abstract: For purposes of scientific investigation and operational monitoring of lakes, we have been testing the application of Coastal Acoustic Tomography (“CAT”) to a deep subtropical lake, Lake Biwa in Japan. This article reports work on measuring nonreciprocity of transmission between transducer pairs, with a final target of assimilating into a 3D hydrodynamic model of the lake.

articleTitle: Assessment of Vessel Noise Impact on Finless Porpoises in the West Part of the Seto Inland Sea, Japan
abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a new type of marine pollution that impacts marine life. It is essential to accurately assess and mitigate its effects on each species. In coastal waters with heavy vessel traffic, noise impacts are a particular concern, and immediate impact assessments are needed for species living in these areas. The narrow-ridged finless porpoise Neophocaena asiaeorientalis sunameri, a small cetacean species, is found in the coastal waters of East Asia. Therefore, they are vulnerable to the effect of vessel noise. However, knowledge regarding these effects is limited. This study aimed to determine the time interval after vessel passage at which click trains of narrow-ridged finless porpoises, inhabiting the western part of the Seto Inland Sea, Japan, were first detected using fixed passive acoustic monitoring data. Furthermore, the effect of vessel presence or absence on the detection of click trains was investigated, along with the correlation between the number of vessels and the number of detected click trains. Fixed passive acoustic monitoring was conducted intermittently using an event recorder, A-tag, from July 2021 to January 2024. The click trains were most frequently detected within 0 to 5 minutes after the vessel passed, while detection rates decreased and remained relatively stable beyond 5 minutes. The detections were increased in the presence of vessel noise. In this study, no acoustically distinct avoidance behavior in response to vessels was observed. After the reduction of noise following vessel passage, the porpoises may increase their click train emission rates, possibly as a form of vigilance or a strategy to detect environmental disturbances caused by the vessels.

articleTitle: FEM-Based Study for Development of Prototype Underwater Acoustic Vector Sensor with integrated Vibration Noise Cancellation
abstract: This study investigates various design parameters for the development of an underwater Acoustic Vector Sensor (AVS) with an integrated vibration noise cancellation mechanism, aimed at enhancing the performance of AVS extensively used in marine research, underwater navigation, and military applications. AVS measures sound field information in terms of pressure and particle velocity along three orthogonal axes. The two primary types of AVS configurations exist are P-P (pressure gradient type) and P-U (hydrophone and particle velocity transducer type). The P-U type offers a higher signal-to-noise ratio and frequency-independent beam pattern, making it more suitable for various applications than P-P. However, structural vibrations from mounting platforms such as Autonomous Under-water Vehicles (AUVs) can introduce unwanted noise, affecting measurement accuracy. Therefore, to address this problem, we have proposed the development of a prototype underwater AVS incorporating integrated vibration noise cancellation. This study utilizes the COMSOL Multiphysics software for Finite Element Method (FEM) method to investigate the suitable design parameters and explore the incorporation of an inertial sensor as a secondary sensor to capture platform-induced vibrations. The inertial sensor provides a reference signal that aids in cancelling out the vibration interference from the acoustic measurements. Key objectives include acoustic isolation of the secondary sensor and optimal sensor placement across a frequency range of up to 5 kHz. Different materials—nylon, titanium, stainless steel, visco-elastic rubber, and air are analyzed for their ability to isolate desired acoustic signals to get coupled to a secondary sensor, with simulations calculating the amount of incident energy coupled to the sensor. Additionally, various materials are tested as suitable outer casing. The study presents findings on the optimal material and placement for the secondary sensor and outer casing, providing insights into optimal prototype design for vibration noise cancellation for AVS applications.

articleTitle: Processing and Analysis of Phase-Locked Cavitation Images on a Marine Propeller Surface
abstract: Propeller cavitation has long been a key field of research in marine propulsion systems. This paper presents the processing and analysis of a series of cavitation images acquired by a phase-locked digital imaging system, which was integrated with a cavitation tunnel for open-water tests of a marine propeller. Effective procedures of algorithms of processing and analysis suitable for propeller's cavitation images were developed to extract parameterized characteristics of cavitation. The final results can be expected to be used for validating corresponding numerical simulations and further advancing the propeller's design.

articleTitle: A SiPM-Based Optical Modem for Underwater Wireless Communication: Experiments in Turbid Waters
abstract: The high bandwidth capability of optical wireless communication has sparked interest in underwater applications. Communication links beyond 100 meters can be established in clear waters, supporting the adoption of optics in short-range operations. While the level of water clarity highly affects the maximum transmission range, the type of photodetector used to receive the transmitted light also plays a significant role. In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of using a sensitive silicon photomultiplier (SiPM). The latter is integrated as part of a bidirectional optical modem using 450 nm blue LEDs as the transmitting light source. Experiments conducted near a harbor in Oslofjord, Norway, are compared to a channel model for both daytime and nighttime conditions. During the day under a clear sky, the sea trials resulted in a bit error rate (BER) of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.21 \ \mathrm{x} 10^{-3}$</tex> at 15 meters for a 1 Mbps NRZ-OOK modulated signal. In the evening, with reduced ambient noise, the optical modem achieved a transmission distance of up to 18 meters with a BER of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.85 \ \mathrm{x}\ 10^{-3}$</tex> in the turbid harbor.

articleTitle: Survey of the Tsuzuraozaki Underwater Archaeological Site Using Hovering Type Autonomous Underwater Vehicle
abstract: Many pottery have been discovered in the waters around Tsuzuraozaki, which is located on the northern shore of Lake Biwa in Shiga Prefecture. However the cause of the archaeological site has not yet been determined, because of the depth and high turbidity of the water, it is difficult for divers to investigate the area. Therefore, in December 2023, we conducted an observation survey of the lake bed by mounting a camera on an Autonomous Underwater Vehicle Tuna-Sand2. We created a mosaic image by enhancing the image with Malti-Scale Retinex and pasting it along the trajectory of the AUV. The survey results showed the location of the pottery-like objects and the surrounding terrain. However, it is difficult to determine from the image whether the object is pottery or not, and in which period it was made. In future research, we aim to delve deeper into the intricacies of the objects found in this survey. In addition, it is also essential to have a technology that can remove floating matter from images of water with high turbidity.

articleTitle: Development of a Remotely Operated Vehicle with Underwater Cleaning Capabilities Using a Systems Engineering Approach
abstract: In recent years, the global wind power generation and marine development industries have seen significant technological advancements. The maintenance and cleaning of offshore facilities are essential tasks. Traditional manual diving operations are not only costly but also entail high risks, making the use of Remotely Operated Underwater Vehicles (ROVs) crucial for assisting in various operations. The objective of this study is to develop a prototype ROV capable of cleaning marine growth from offshore wind turbine foundations. By applying a systems engineering approach to the development process, the study follows rigorous procedures including requirements verification, conceptual design, preliminary design, detailed design, manufacturing and assembly, system integration, and testing and validation. This process successfully results in the development of a prototype ROV with underwater cleaning capabilities. During the development process, we divided the work into four main categories: mechanical structure system, Human-Machine Interface (HMI) system, power system, and system integration. The design of the mechanical structure system considers the stability and durability required for underwater operations, ensuring that the ROV can operate continuously in various marine environments. The HMI system focuses on developing an intuitive and easy-to-operate control interface for the operator, enhancing the flexibility and precision of operation. The power system is designed to provide stable power supply in different mission scenarios, ensuring continuous power support for the ROV during long-duration operations. Finally, system integration is responsible for effective synchronization and collaboration between subsystems to achieve the intended goals. This study leverages the advantages of the systems engineering approach in equipment system development projects, successfully developing a prototype of ROV with underwater cleaning capabilities. This provides a more efficient and safer solution for the maintenance of offshore facilities, achieving benefits such as extending the service life of offshore equipment, reducing costs, and protecting the safety of operators. The research results have significant practical value for industrial applications.

articleTitle: Assessing Taiwan's Coral Reef Ecosystem: Detecting Long-term Snapping Shrimp Sounds
abstract: Snap sounds, which constitute primary components of underwater soundscapes, serve as crucial indicators of ecosystem health. However, reliable detection of these acoustic signatures presents significant challenges, as methods relying solely on amplitude thresholds often result in overestimation of snap rates. This study presents a time-series data processing approach that integrates amplitude thresholds with kurtosis measurements to improve the accuracy of snap sound detection. Analysis of recordings from Taiwan's marine protected areas revealed predominantly low kurtosis values, highlighting the analytical challenges inherent in complex coral reef ecosystems. Through comparative analysis with manually verified snap sounds, kurtosis thresholds provide stricter and more accurate identification of snap sounds. Additionally, compared to smoothed kernel methods, kurtosis thresholds more effectively exclude non-snap signals. This improved detection approach enhances the robustness of quantifying snap rate variations, thereby improving ecosystem assessments and supporting more effective conservation strategies.

articleTitle: A Low-cost, Expendable Shallow Water Profiling Float with Improved Capabilities
abstract: Floats are underwater drifting buoys and are being used extensively for oceanographic measurements. For example, the Argo program employs over 4000 floats annually for ocean observation and they measure temperature, pressure and salinity that contributes data to climate change studies. The program also employs biogeochemical floats that measure chlorophyll, Nitrate, Oxygen, pH and suspended particles in the ocean water column. Nevertheless, they are expensive when sourced in small quantities and has limited capabilities per float. Availability of low-cost sensors and electronic modules have made it possible to drive down the cost of floats. In this paper we report design and development of a low-cost float with enhanced capabilities for use in oceanographic research. Apart from the traditional sensors like temperature, pressure and conductivity, the shallow water profiling device (SPD) described in this paper is equipped with an echo sounder to measure bathymetry and a hydrophone to measure the ambient noise. The system has a depth capability of 200m and an endurance of 100 profiling cycles. Pre-processed data are transmitted via a satellite link and presented to the end user through a graphical interface. Results from experiments conducted in local waters are provided in support of the equipment capability. The low cost of the system means it can be expendable at the end of its life, if desired to reduce the environmental impact arising from its recovery operations.

articleTitle: Development of a Time-Synchronized Projector-Camera System for High-Clarity Underwater Imaging
abstract: We developed a time-synchronized projectorcamera system (SyncProCam) for high-clarity underwater imaging. The proposed system uses a rolling shutter camera and a laser projector, synchronized via a custom-designed digital circuit to capture only direct light reflected from the target. The timesynchronous circuit was implemented using an FPGA, which includes an IIR filter to remove noise and irrelevant signal components from the projector's MEMS mirror signal and a digital circuit to detect the projector's scanning start timing. These components enabled the successful generation of temporally precise camera trigger signals. Experimental results in turbid water environments demonstrate that the standalone SyncProCam enhances image clarity compared to generalpurpose cameras.

articleTitle: Using ROVs for Tilt Angle Measurement of Pier Foundation Piles at Pier-Type Docks
abstract: Regular inspection of pier foundation piles is essential for ensuring the structural integrity and operational safety of pier-type docks. Traditional approaches rely on divers to manually measure pile tilt angles using inclinometers, but these methods pose significant safety risks and are increasingly constrained by the dwindling availability of skilled divers. This study investigates the use of remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) equipped with advanced sonar technology as a safer, more efficient alternative for underwater pile inspections. A mini-ROV outfitted with dual-frequency forward-looking sonar (FLS) and supplementary sensors was employed, with the sonar system mounted vertically to facilitate tilt angle measurements through edge detection of sonar images. To enhance the robustness of data processing under complex underwater environments, algorithmic improvements in noise suppression and edge detection were implemented. Field experiments conducted at Xingda Harbor in Taiwan involved inspecting 65 pier foundation piles. The ROV's sonar-based measurements were compared to diver-acquired tilt angles, which served as the ground truth. Results revealed that the ROV method achieved an average error of −1.37 degrees, with final error rates remaining within 4% after compensating for ROV attitude changes. These findings confirm that the ROV-based approach delivers accuracy comparable to traditional diver methods while significantly reducing operational risks and reliance on human divers. This study underscores the potential of ROVs to revolutionize underwater inspections, offering a safe and efficient solution for real-world applications.

articleTitle: Design of Communication Circuits for Underwater Wireless Communication Utilizing Ion Wave
abstract: Underwater wireless communication is essential for various marine applications, such as exploration and monitoring. However, existing methods, including acoustic, optical, and electromagnetic waves, have limitations in enclosed environments. This research proposes a new underwater wireless communication system utilizing electrical conductivity of seawater. This method employs ion plasma wave propagation, offering a potential alternative for reliable communication in electrically isolated spaces. The study investigated the feasibility and performance of this method through experiments in controlled environments. Previous tests in a polyvinyl chloride pipe demonstrated the influence of salt concentration on signal intensity, suggesting the role of ion plasma waves. To enhance transmission efficiency, the research focused on optimizing the communication circuits. By incorporating a transformer on the transmission side and a band-pass filter on the reception side, communication over 15 meters was achieved with a significantly reduced input voltage of 5 V, compared to 50 V used in previous studies. Further experiments explored vertical signal propagation, revealing limitations in depth compared to horizontal transmission. The findings suggest that the proposed ion wave communication method holds promising potential for underwater applications in confined spaces. Future research directions include further optimization of the circuits, a thorough investigation of the communication principles, and exploration of signal propagation characteristics in diverse underwater environments.

articleTitle: Particle Filter Based Estimation of Mn-Crust Layers in Sub-Bottom Sonar Data
abstract: Cobalt-rich manganese crust (Mn-crust) is a deep sea mineral resource being targeted as a source of critical minerals. Estimating the volumetric distribution of Mn-crust requires measuring its thickness and lateral distribution. Acoustic in-situ methods are proven to be effective for continuous thickness measurements suitable for volumetric estimation. In order to address the challenges in thickness measurement in the presence of noise, this paper proposes a new Bayesian estimator using particle filter in order to detect the reflections in sub-bottom acoustic data. The algorithm developed is applied to field collected data from deep sea surveys of Autonomous Underwater Vehicle BossA. The feasibility of the proposed method is described along with challenges and future research directions.

articleTitle: Development of a Deep Sea Remote Experiment System for Visualizing Methane Bubbles Behavior in Hydrate Environment
abstract: As part of the research and development of shallow methane hydrate recovery and production technologies for deep-sea environments, the potential use of membrane structures for capturing methane seeps while mining and for pollution prevention to reduce environmental impact of mining has been investigated. In our previous study, we developed a visualization system that replicates the methane hydrate environment on the seafloor in a laboratory setting. This system has been utilized to conduct numerous laboratory experiments, providing insights into the behavior of methane bubbles with a hydrate film on their surface. These bubbles differ from conventional methane bubbles in their interaction with various membrane materials. The pure water is utilized in these experiments to eliminate the impact of complex variables present in sea water, such as dissolved gases, ions, and particles. To validate the applicability of the obtained characteristics to the actual sea environment, comparison tests should be conducted in the deep sea, where methane hydrate exists. In this study, we have developed a deep sea remote experiment system that has capabilities to execute analogous tests in situ within a deep sea environment. The design of the system and some results obtained at depths of approximately 1000 meters are presented in this paper.

articleTitle: Multi-AUV-based Marine Survey for Advanced Underwater Exploration
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to marine surveys using multiple autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), developed and implemented by the National Maritime Research Institute of Japan. By leveraging the collective capabilities of multiple AUVs, this methodology enables highly efficient, high-resolution seafloor surveys with exceptional reliability. Key innovations include advanced multi-vehicle coordination techniques for real-time position adjustment, significantly enhancing the quality of acoustic bottom surveys. These techniques are integrated into an on-site adaptive motion planning framework, which dynamically responds to the changing conditions of multi-AUV operations. Another notable feature is the simplicity of the approach, ensuring ease of use across various AUV systems and user applications. Additionally, the paper explores state-of-the-art advancements in underwater docking and on-site data transfer by multiple AUVs, paving the way for reliable, long-term underwater exploration. These innovations collectively establish a foundation for advancing marine survey capabilities in diverse underwater environments.

articleTitle: Development of Detection Method for CO2 Seepage in the Ocean Using Machine Learning
abstract: CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> seepage detection from the seabed in carbon storage projects is crucial, but conventional methods based on the relationship between dissolved oxygen saturation and CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> partial pressure have resulted in false detections. This study aimed to develop an accurate seepage detection method using machine learning models. We collected 66 seepage data points from natural seepage in Tachibana Bay and artificial seepage off Tateyama, along with 502 non-seepage data points from the Tomakomai demonstration project and other sources. Three machine learning models-Local Outlier Factor, One Class Support Vector Machine, and Random Forest-were evaluated for performance. Random Forest demonstrated superior accuracy. While optimizing input feature combinations enabled more accurate seepage detection compared to conventional indicators, the imbalanced dataset (11.6 % seepage, 88.4 % non-seepage) remains a challenge requiring further data collection.

articleTitle: Distributed Optical Fiber Sensing in Scientific Deep Seafloor Borehole Observatory in the Nankai Trough
abstract: The Nankai Trough hosts diverse seismic phenomena across various timescales, requiring deep borehole observatories for comprehensive monitoring. In addition to the seafloor borehole observatories constructed in IODP NantroSEIZE project, we developed a new optical fiber-based borehole observation system, integrated with the DONET submarine cable network. In November 2023, a 500 m deep borehole observatory (C9038B) was installed off the Kii Channel, enabling real-time monitoring of strain and pore-fluid pressure, for the first implementation of such seafloor borehole observation system. In October 2024, we successfully conducted distributed optical fiber sensing (DOFS) in the borehole for the first time by compensating optical losses with amplifier systems. Both Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) and Rayleigh Frequency Acoustic and Strain (RFAS) techniques provided detailed insights into strain variations induced by microseisms and tidal fluctuations at the borehole situated in the front of Nankai Trough subduction.

articleTitle: Seafloor Crustal Deformation Observations Utilizing Unmanned Surface Vehicles for Monitoring Fault Locking and Sliding Processes at Subduction Zone Plate Boundaries
abstract: While positioning on the seafloor is difficult by means of the global navigation satellite system (GNSS), GNSS-Acoustic (GNSS-A) technique is a powerful tool to detect the seafloor crustal deformation associated with mega-thrust earthquakes that occur in the plate subduction zones. We have been using an unmanned surface vehicle (USV), Wave Glider, as a sea surface platform to perform GNSS-A observations since 2019 and detected the post-seismic deformation of the 2011 Tohoku-oki earthquake along the Japan Trench. Based on the knowledge obtained from the months-long observation campaigns conducted since 2020, the performance required of USVs to perform GNSS-A observations and future prospects are summarized.

articleTitle: Towards Semi Real-Time Environmental Monitoring Using Shadowgraphy
abstract: Environmental monitoring for detecting habitat changes as well as for mining impact assessment has become a crucial topic in recent years. This requires large-scale spatial and temporal data collection for analysis. At JAMSTEC, we have been working on the development of shadowgraph-based imaging systems to address this issue. Shadowgraph-based imaging systems consume low amounts of power and are not affected by external lighting conditions, making them ideal for monitoring. Also, since shadowgraphs use collimated light, it is easy to extract particle sizes along with particle counts. We have developed multiple inhouse shadowgraph systems with different viewing areas and resolutions for different monitoring requirements. A data processing pipeline has been made which can analyze the shadowgraph videos post-cruise and analyze plankton distributions and abundances as well as provide other information such as particle distributions, size distributions and detect events such as plumes and mixing layers using pattern matching. Since the shadowgraph videos can contain a large variety of animals, we are also using human-in-the-loop machine learning for training target-specific models based on the target assessment. The system has been installed on various underwater platforms, such as a long-term seafloor lander as well as CTD-rosette systems. We are now developing an extension to the system that can provide near real-time feedback to the host platform based on the survey results. We aim to provide alerts when particular events and observations are detected, which can be customized based on the monitoring targets. In the future, we are planning to integrate these shadowgraphs with other underwater platforms such as AUVs and seafloor stations.

articleTitle: A Novel Underwater Biomimetic Propulsion System Derived from Zebrafish Neurological Analysis
abstract: We propose a biomimetic propulsion system inspired by the spinal motor control mechanisms of zebrafish, allowing the submersible to adapt its propulsion strategy in real time based on real-time feedback from the environment. The design consists of two components: a neurological model and a topological model. The topological model is derived from Navier-Stokes equations to simulate fluid dynamics, coupled with topology optimization methods to optimize the shape and surface interactions of the submersible with water. To evaluate the effectiveness of the system, we tested the system under two control conditions: open-loop configurations and closed configurations. The experimental results demonstrated that the topology and topological mod-els achieved significant improvements in energy efficiency and traversal time, compared to a control set-up. This design allows us to extend the operational range and duration of underwater vehicles, enabling more extensive and sustainable exploration of the ocean floor. This technology has far-reaching implications for ocean exploration, climate research, and underwater robotics. Moreover, the scalability of our design allows for potential applications in larger underwater vehicles as well as in multi-agent systems where multiple underwater vehicles work together.

articleTitle: Lifting and Mooring Mechanism for a Surface Vehicle Equipped with an Underwater Vehicle
abstract: The development of underwater vehicles has advanced significantly, but challenges such as operational efficiency, transportability, and the need for specialized equipment remain. This study aims to develop a surface vehicle equipped with a lifting and mooring mechanism that can deploy, retrieve, and tether an underwater vehicle efficiently. The surface vehicle is designed for easy transport by a few people, with features such as modular components and maneuverability for versatile deployment. The lifting and mooring mechanism employs a magnetic coupling system, enabling compact design and scalability for additional functionalities. Experimental evaluations demonstrated the mechanism's ability to lift loads between 30 kg and 35 kg, confirming its capacity to handle the 7 kg underwater vehicle effectively.

articleTitle: Do Offshore Wind Farms at Miaoli Cause Acoustic Deterrence to White Dolphin and Fish? Reveals a Short-Term Study at Taiwan Strait
abstract: Passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) was deployed at three locations (Miaoli, Taichung, and Changhua) along the Taiwan Strait for seven days to study marine soundscapes. The acoustic data analysis revealed biophony from Sousa chinensis taiwanensis. (the Taiwanese White Dolphins, TWD), diurnal chorusing from two types of fish, and one unidentified cetacean (possibly false killer whale or Indo-Pacific finless porpoise). The main anthropogenic contribution at these sites originated from persistent vessel movements and continuous low-frequency (10-200 Hz) noise. Results demonstrated higher low-frequency sound levels and vessel detection rates in the Miaoli area compared to Taichung and Changhua. A reduced number of fish chorusing was observed in the Miaoli area, while no acoustic activity from TWD was detected. Additionally, through a workshop gathering feedback on current underwater noise guidelines, experts provided recommendations from environmental protection, technical measurement, and regulatory perspectives, emphasizing the impacts of pile driving noise on dolphin metabolism and vocalization, as well as the necessity of lifecycle noise management for wind farms. The short-term soundscape monitoring results presented in this study indicate elevated noise levels at Miaoli, potentially associated with offshore wind farm-related activities, affecting both fish vocalization and TWD activities.

articleTitle: Measurements of Differential Acoustic Travel Times at a Carrier Frequency of 5 kHz in a River Reach at a Range of 1.13 km
abstract: We report a simple validation experiment for measurement of “differential travel time” (DTT) between acoustic transducers separated by 1.13 km in a river reach of depth about 7. <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$7\mathrm{m}$</tex>. Good correlation is found between the currents estimated from DTT and the cross-sectional bulk velocity, but DTT -based path-averaged current is about 30% greater than cross-sectional average. This difference is probably due to concentration of current velocity toward the vertical plane of the river thalweg, through which the received sound passed.

articleTitle: Collision Avoidance Method for USVs Based on the Artificial Potential Field and Elliptical Ship Domain
abstract: With the rapid development of unmanned vehicle technology, the shipping industry is facing increasingly severe navigation safety challenges. The significant increase in the number of ships at sea has made ports and waterways more congested. To address this, the International Maritime Organization has formulated the COLREGs to promote coordination and consensus in collision avoidance processes. However, approximately 80% of maritime accidents are caused by human error, highlighting the importance of developing unmanned surface vehicles (USVs). USVs can not only assist tugboats and pilots with boarding operations but also reduce the risk of human error. The APF method has been widely applied in collision avoidance technology for unmanned vehicles. APF technology transforms navigation into a potential field model, allowing ships to autonomously avoid obstacles. However, the traditional artificial potential field method often results in longer collision avoidance paths in dynamic environments or high-density navigation areas, thereby increasing risk. To solve this problem, this paper proposes an improved method based on the artificial potential field to guide ship collision avoidance. This method creates an elliptical field at the collision point of two ships. As the distance between the own ship and the collision point decreases, the semi-minor axis of the elliptical field lengthens. An attractive point is set at the edge of the semi-minor axis. The attractive force generated by this point and the repulsive force generated by the collision point overlap, forming a resultant force to guide the ship in collision avoidance. Compared to the traditional artificial potential field method without an attractive point, the improved method proposed in this work can reduce the collision avoidance path length by 12-24%. Most importantly, this method complies with COLREGs regulations, enabling quick alignment with existing ship collision avoidance rules and ensuring consistency. This improvement enhances the collision avoidance performance of unmanned vehicles.

articleTitle: Enhancing the Searching Efficiency of Flight Recorder Through the Near Real-Time Localization
abstract: The Underwater Locator Beacon (ULB), attached to flight recorders, transmits continuous signals upon water immersion to aid in recovery operations. Timely localization is critical due to the limited operational lifespans of ULBs: 30 days for DK120 (37.5 kHz) and 90 days for DK180 (8.8 kHz). This study developed a near-real-time localization system using a towed hydrophone array to detect ULB signals and dynamically adjust search operations. Field experiments were conducted off the coast of Liuqiu Island under varying ocean currents and vessel speeds to evaluate the system's performance. Results demonstrated the adaptability and stability of the system, significantly enhancing search efficiency. By incorporating real-time feedback from electronic compasses, accelerometers, and depth sensors, the heading and attitude of the towed array were accurately monitored, reducing bearing angle errors. Dynamic heading correction reduced positioning errors from 650 meters to 70 meters during operations, demonstrating the critical role of real-time attitude correction in underwater localization. The workflow integrated three key steps: (1) drop point analysis to estimate the search area using radar disappearance points and acoustic modeling, (2) near-real-time localization using TDOA-based signal processing and grid probability statistical methods, and (3) dynamic route adjustment to narrow the search area and focus resources. The DK180's 8.8 kHz signal was particularly effective in deep-sea environments, offering longer transmission ranges and higher signal-to-noise ratios than the DK120. This study's findings highlight the potential of near-real-time localization systems to improve search and rescue operations for flight recorders, enhancing both efficiency and positioning accuracy in underwater environments.

articleTitle: Behavior Trees for Adaptive Multi-sensor Perception in Autonomous Underwater Robotics
abstract: Behavior trees (BTs) have recently shown great promise in improving how robotic systems make decisions and execute tasks. Building on such successes, this study explores the potential application of BTs for multi-sensor perception in autonomous underwater robots. We discuss a framework in which BTs could enable subsea robots to adapt to the ever-changing conditions underwater through an intelligent combination and coordination of multiple sensor types. Through several case studies, we illustrate the capabilities of this approach for enabling marine robots to become more reliable and flexible, improving their ability to safely navigate, detect objects, and map environments. While the implementation and experimental validation of this framework are reserved for future work, we argue that BTs can significantly boost the autonomy and resilience of underwater robots, leading to smarter and more capable systems for exploring and working underwater.

articleTitle: Efficient Parameter Determination for BPDN in Underwater Acoustic MIMO-OSDM Communications Using Stein's Unbiased Risk Estimate
abstract: Underwater acoustic (UWA) communication schemes including multiple-input-multiple-output orthogonal signal division multiplexing (MIMO-OSDM) are crucial for the wireless operation of autonomous unmanned vehicles and remotely operated vehicles. This paper presents an efficient regularization parameter determination for MIMO-OSDM to design a reliable communication system. Recent studies have revealed that utilizing sparsity, a physical nature of the UWA channel can improve communication quality. While the combination of MIMO-OSDM and basis pursuit denoising (BPDN) enables the UWA communication that accounts for channel sparsity, this approach requires the prior simulation to obtain a database to fine-tune linear coefficients which decide the regularization parameter of BPDN. To reduce computational cost without sacrificing communication quality, we propose the statistical solution: an application of Stein's unbiased risk estimate (SURE) for MIMO-OSDM using BPDN aiming for parameter determination through a minimization of the channel estimation error. Our simulation results demonstrated that the proposed parameter determinator serves as an estimator of channel estimation error. Our experimental results demonstrated that the proposed channel estimator using SURE achieved almost the same communication quality and demodulation performance as the existing method without prior database creation.

articleTitle: Navigating Uncertainty: Application of Information Theory for Ocean Exploration Using AUV
abstract: Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) encounter significant challenges in effectively navigating and mapping underwater environments, primarily due to the uncertainties and limitations associated with onboard sensors. These limitations are compounded by the inherent constraints of AUV endurance when tasked with exploring vast underwater regions. Hence, efficient search strategies are critical for locating objects of interest, such as mines, shipwrecks, or plane debris, in marine environments. To tackle these challenges, this study proposes an innovative search methodology that leverages information theoretic concepts such as Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and discrimination gain to intelligently explore areas in presence of poor sensor accuracy. The presented method guides the search by quantifying the expected reduction in uncertainty and improving decision-making based on the prior observations. In essence, the presented framework is designed to enhance search performance in scenarios with low-quality sensors characterized by lowered probabilities of true positives and increased probabilities of false alarms. By leveraging information theory, this study demonstrates that the proposed probabilistic approach outperforms traditional sweep search methods. Monte Carlo simulations across various scenarios are conducted to evaluate detection accuracy, exploration-to-exploitation balance, and the number of moves required for successful mine detection. Results highlight the robustness of the proposed method, particularly in terrains with significant variability, offering a practical solution for real-world applications like mine detection and underwater archaeology.

articleTitle: Implementation and Application of a Knowledge Service for AUV Mission Explainability
abstract: This paper presents a knowledge service aimed at enhancing mission explainability in subsea robotics operations. The proposed system consists of an AI agent that chains together specialized large language models (LLMs) and a graph database to enable natural language querying and interactive visualization. The graph database models entities and relationships relevant to subsea inspection and maintenance, such as clients, industries, sites, vehicles, sensors, and underwater scene elements, including pipeline components and seafloor characteristics. The browser-based GUI aims to allow stakeholders—including field teams, robot developers, industry clients, and regulatory agencies—to intuitively interact with mission data, supporting post-mission analysis and explainability. Using pipeline inspections as a case study, we illustrate the potential of this approach and discuss future developments needed to advance this framework toward a practical solution for subsea robotics.

articleTitle: Operational Space Fomulation of Time Delay Control for Underwater Vehicles and its Extension to Diver Guidance
abstract: In this study, we propose a method for designing a robust controller for underwater vehicles when the control input space and workspace differ. To achieve this, we formulate the Time Delay Control (TDC) in operational space, which is efficient yet has a simple structure. The proposed controller maintains the robustness against disturbances and structural simplicity inherent in the conventional TDC while effectively addressing the situation where the workspace differs from the control input space. Additionally, we propose a method for applying the proposed controller to the task of guiding divers to their destinations using underwater vehicles. Underwater environments often have limited visibility due to issues such as turbidity, so we design the controller and reference trajectories based on the diver's field of view. Through simulations, we demonstrate that the proposed control method effectively operates in various workspaces, including world-coordinate-based workspaces and diver's field of view-based workspaces.

articleTitle: Constraining Acoustic Positioning with Vehicle Measurements from an Underwater Glider
abstract: Broadband acoustic transmissions from five moored transceivers were received by two autonomous Seagliders in August 2017 during the Canada Basin Acoustic Propagation Experiment. Long-range acoustic data from these receptions were utilized in a least squares inversion to obtain subsurface position estimates. Acoustic sources in this experiment did not transmit simultaneously and in some cases, position estimates spanned larger distances during the reception period than expected given typical horizontal vehicle speeds. Horizontal speeds derived from vehicle measurements can be used to impose a physical limit on the position estimation. Here, three iterations of the least squares model, using increasingly more vehicle data, are presented for two example acoustic receptions received on a Seaglider. The final iteration demonstrates how in situ vehicle measurements can be used to refine position estimates from long-range acoustic data.

articleTitle: Comparison of Regularization Methods for Multipath Mitigation in Mirror- Type Coastal Acoustic Tomography
abstract: This study addresses a significant challenge in mirror-type coastal acoustic tomographic (MCAT) systems: the accurate extraction of travel-time information from signals af-fected by multipath interference. While MCAT enables real-time monitoring of ocean currents, multipath propagation in coastal environments can severely reduce measurement accuracy, particularly for non-primary acoustic arrivals. We investigate two regularization methods- Tikhonov (TK) and total variation (TV)-to mitigate this interference and enhance the precision of travel-time estimation. Through systematic numerical simulations and Monte Carlo analysis, we evaluate these methods under varying signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions ranging from −5 to 5 dB. Our results reveal distinct performance characteristics for each approach. TK regularization demonstrates superior accuracy in moderate to high SNR environments (greater than 3 dB), achieving correlation coefficients exceeding 0.93 compared to ground truth measurements. This makes TK particularly suitable for typical MCAT operational conditions, where SNR often exceeds 10 dB. In contrast, TV regularization maintains consis-tent performance across all SNR levels, although its correlation coefficients range from 0.58 to 0.73. This provides reliable measurements even in challenging noisy conditions. These findings offer important methodological guidance for signal processing in MCAT systems, allowing for optimal technique selection based on environmental conditions. For standard operations with good signal quality, TK regularization provides superior precision, while TV regularization serves as a robust alternative in more challenging environments. This research enhances ocean monitoring capabilities by establishing a framework to mitigate multipath interference in MCAT systems.

articleTitle: Identifying and Classifying Whale Sounds in Underwater Soundscapes Based on Faster Regionbased Convolutional Neural Networks
abstract: Passive acoustic monitoring is a well-established tool for studying underwater soundscapes, including ship noise, the activity and ecology of marine animal species. As people pay more and more attention to marine ecology and the amount of passive acoustic data collected increases exponentially, an efficient detection model is needed to assist in the analysis of underwater acoustic data. This study proposes Faster R-CNN to identify the sounds of Chinese white dolphins in 36 hours of acoustic data collected at a monitoring point off the coast of Yunlin, Taiwan. The model had an average accuracy of 0.87 and an average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${0. 8 0 2}$</tex>. This model output was used to analyze the spatial and temporal patterns of Chinese white dolphin calls, confirming the behavioral patterns of Chinese white dolphins living near Taiwan. This study demonstrates that Faster R-CNN trained on a small data set generalizes well to highly variable signal types under various recording and noise conditions. We demonstrate the utility of transfer learning methods. These results validate the feasibility of applying deep learning models to identify highly variable signals across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales, enabling new discoveries by combining large datasets with cutting-edge tools.

articleTitle: Tracking Error Based Fault Tolerant Scheme for Marine Vehicles with Thruster Redundancy
abstract: This paper proposes an active model-based fault and failure tolerant control scheme for a class of marine vehicles with thruster redundancy. Unlike widely used state and parameter estimation methods, where the estimation errors are utilized to generate residual, in this paper we directly apply the trajectory tracking error terms to construct residual and detect thruster fault and failure in the steady state of the tracking system. As for identification or diagnosis, this paper proposes a novel scheme through a detailed examination of the tracking error trends and the combinations of thruster configurations. Since this fault detection and identification operates within the same closed-loop of the tracking control system, control reconfiguration can be easily achieved by adjusting the weight parameter of the isolated thruster to minimize tracking errors or residual. Numerical studies with the real world vehicle model is also carried out to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.

articleTitle: Using Underwater Hyperspectral Imaging to Increase Feature Detection and Improve Under-Ice Navigation
abstract: Extensive sea ice in Arctic marine regions has hindered indepth exploration and research. To overcome this frontier, underwater robots are increasingly used to explore beneath the ice cover. While this enables research over a broader area, it increases the risk of losing valuable vehicles under the ice, placing greater emphasis on the navigational capabilities of the robots. While inertial and acoustical navigation methods share limitations for operating under the ice, visual navigation can utilize optical features for position estimation at a very fine resolution. However, the underside of ice tends to lack visible features. To overcome this, we propose integrating a novel Underwater Hyperspectral Imager. This technology captures detailed spectral information, revealing features and patterns invisible to traditional imaging methods. To test this, a Remotely Operated Vehicle was equipped with an upward-pointing hyperspectral imager. Three Arctic expeditions were conducted, capturing under-ice data including an Arctic ice algae bloom. To determine whether the hyperspectral imager provides improved navigation capabilities, we created five spectral transformations utilizing the spectral quantity of the hyperspectral domain by either increasing the number of layers fed into the detection algorithm (5-Band, 10-Band and 20-band) or by transforming the spectra using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and the Pearson correlation. We then compared these to four transformations which resembled the behaviour of an RGB/grayscale equivalent. We found that the hyperspectral methods showed an improvement in precision. These improvements in precision highlight the potential of hyperspectral imagina for robust navigation in challenging under-ice environments.

articleTitle: Adaptive Informative Path Planning for Lightweight AUV in Coastal Benthic Environments
abstract: Efficient coastal benthic monitoring requires au-tonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) that can systematically survey areas while adaptively investigating features of interest. Traditional coverage planning methods follow fixed patterns that may miss important targets or waste resources on less informative regions. This paper presents a reinforcement learning approach to adaptive informative path planning (AIPP) that unifies coverage completion with target detection objectives. Our framework combines a carefully structured reward mechanism with a novel local view feature extraction method to enable ef-ficient exploration and target investigation. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves 97.8 % coverage rate and 87.9% detection efficiency across 1000 simulated test scenarios, with a 97.3% task success rate. The framework shows particular strength in environments with patchy target distributions, typical of coastal benthic ecosystems. While simulation results are promising, we identify key challenges in parameter optimization and uncertainty handling that must be addressed for real-world deployment. This work establishes a foundation for more efficient autonomous benthic observation systems that can effectively balance systematic coverage with adaptive information gathering.

articleTitle: Salp Swarm Algorithm Based Fractional Order PID Controller Design for Trajectory Tracking Simulation of an Underactuated Underwater Vehicle Model
abstract: Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) are used in many fields, primarily in scientific, commercial, and military areas. These vehicles require various guidance and control systems to autonomously perform tasks underwater. The modeling, system identification, and control of AUVs remain active areas of research and development. In this study, modelling and trajectory tracking simulation of a low-speed, modular, symmetrical and underactuated underwater vehicle with 4DOF are evaluated. The vehicle, named RedFin is developed in Kocaeli University Laboratories. Dynamical model parameters of the AUV's are estimated by Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and analytical calculation techniques and the AUV mathematical model is obtained. Model validation was carried out through static and dynamic pool tests. control algorithm has been developed, offering more precise solutions. For dynamic models described by fractional differential equations, a Fractional Order PID (FOPID) control algorithm was developed, offering more precise solutions. In the study, a PID controller and a FOPID controller were designed for the trajectory tracking control of the AUV. The Salp Swarm Algorithm (SSA), one of the heuristic optimization algorithms, is used to optimize the gain parameters of both controllers. The integral of the absolute value of the position error (IAE) is selected as the fitness function. “Band Limited White Noise” with 0.5 W power and 200 Hz frequency was added to the system model control inputs. During the orbit tracking, the RMS values of depth control errors are very small, such as 0.021 m for SSA-PID, 0.0032 m for GA-KDPID, and 0.00118 m for SSA-KDPID.

articleTitle: Numerical Study for the Variations of Flow Field During FKT Operation
abstract: Taiwan, surrounded by the ocean, benefits from the powerful Kuroshio Current along its eastern coastline, presenting substantial potential for harnessing marine energy resources. To capitalize on these opportunities, the National Academy of Marine Research initiated research and development efforts in 2020, focusing on key technologies for ocean current energy and conducting sea trials. These efforts are expected to culminate in the development of a Floating Kuroshio Turbine (FKT). To gain a comprehensive understanding of the FKT's underwater operations, this study employs a series of numerical simulations. Using the Navier-Stokes equations, combined with the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{k}-\varepsilon$</tex> turbulence model and dynamic mesh techniques, a numerical model for fluid-structure interaction is developed. The simulation results reveal that as flow velocity increases, the vortices behind the unit become increasingly complex. For the 20 kW FKT, the dual-blade system with counter-rotating blades reduces the downstream impact distance compared to a single-unit setup, limiting it to approximately 4 to 5 times the length of the unit's longest side. The primary objective of this study is to enhance understanding of the system's performance under different FKT, providing critical insights for future design optimizations and environmental impact assessments.

articleTitle: Application of Deconvolution Processing in Passive Localization Technology for Circular Array
abstract: In the present study, a robust passive localization technology, based on a uniform circular array and combining beamforming with deconvolution processing, is developed. The goal is to be applicable in low SNR and low snapshot conditions and to be applied to cylindrical sonar systems. The study proposes two deconvolution processing methods and compares them with traditional methods: delay-and-sum beamforming (DSB) and multiple signal classification (MUSIC). The first method uses the Richardson-Lucy (RL) algorithm, a common image enhancement technique in astronomy. The second method use the deconvolution approaches for acoustic source mapping (DAMAS). Both static and dynamic scenarios are used in the simulation. In the static scenario, the array performance of each method is analyzed under different conditions of frequency, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and snapshot. The resolution (main lobe width), main-to-sidelobe ratio (MSR), directivity factor (DF), and localization accuracy are used as quantitative parameters for analysis. In the dynamic scenario, multi-target motion and the Doppler effect are considered to verify the feasibility of the proposed methods. The results show that, compared to the free-space array configuration, the rigid cylinder array configuration offers better MSR and DF. Additionally, the two deconvolution methods proposed in this study indeed exhibit better resolution and localization accuracy than traditional methods.

articleTitle: In Situ Monitoring of the Liquid-Gas Phase Transition for CO2-Rich Fluids Emitted at Deep-Sea Hydrothermal Vent Fields
abstract: One of the promising targets for a deep-sea Raman spectrometer, which enables label-free direct analysis for any phases of targets, is the supercritical and liquid carbon dioxide (sc-/liq-CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) rich fluid spontaneously emitted from hydrothermal vent fields. Sc-/liq-CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) creates a unique dry environment distinct from seawater as a non-aquatic solvent, which could play a potentially significant role in ocean geochemical cycles. In addition, the behaviour of the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-rich fluids in the water column, particularly the water depth of the fluid phase transition from liquid to gas, is important to understand the transport system of the volatiles in the fluids as well as the potential impact on acidification of the water column. However, contamination from the seawater during collection and measurement is unavoidable, and the dynamic phase and compositional changes cannot be measured by sampling-based methods. In this paper, the history of the development of deep-sea Raman spectrometers is first reviewed, and a novel method for sampling and analysing CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-rich fluids in different phases using a deep-sea Raman spectrometer mounted on a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) is reported. In situ monitoring of the phase of liq-CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-rich fluids while the ROV ascended was performed at different hydrothermal ventfields in the Mariana Arc and Okinawa Trough. The in situ Raman measurement revealed that the phase transition occurred at different depths depending on the fluid compositions. The study demonstrates the ability of the Raman spectroscopy to monitor the phase transition of CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-rich. fluids and the chemical composition in real time on site, showing the ability as a novel marine geochemical sensing technique.

articleTitle: From Virtual Waters to Real Oceans: A Simulation-Driven Approach to ROV Control System Design
abstract: In this paper the software-in-the-Ioop (SIL) approach employed at NTNU's Applied Underwater Robotics Lab-oratory (AUR-lab) for developing control system software for underwater vehicles is described. An underwater simulator based on Gazebo is presented, and the software structure that allows us to transition from simulations to field trials is explained. Multiple examples are given of systems that are developed in simulation and then applied to real-world experiments.

articleTitle: Combining Geophysics, Core Sampling, and GIS for Conducting Underwater Archaeology in the Taijiang Inner Sea, Taiwan
abstract: This research aims to detect possible the underwater cultural heritage within the Taijiang Inner Sea, focusing on 17th-century shipwrecks of the Dutch East India Company(VOC). The primary objective is to identify and analyze ferromagnetic materials such as anchors and cannons, which are key indicators of these historic shipwrecks. A comprehensive suite of exploration techniques is employed, including airborne and shipborne magnetometers to detect magnetic anomalies associated with ferromagnetic artifacts. Complementary methods such as side-scan sonar and multibeam bathymetry provide detailed imagery and topographical maps of the riverbed, facilitating precise localization of potential sites. Sub-bottom profiling is utilized to examine sediment layers and identify buried structures, while core sampling offered insights into sediment composition and historical deposition patterns. All collected data are integrated and analyzed with Geographic Information Systems (GIS), enabling the synthesis of multi-source information to create accurate maps of potential shipwreck locations. Through the combined use of airborne and shipborne instruments, the research successfully identified dozens of potential underwater cultural heritage sites. Detailed analysis revealed distinct patterns indicative of historic shipwrecks, distinguishing them from natural features. The classification process refined the potential locations, plotting probable distribution map of various shipwrecks in accordance with historical records, and highlighting regions of significant archaeological interest. These findings contribute substantially to understanding the submerged cultural landscape of the Taijiang Inner Sea, enriching the historical narrative of 17th-century maritime trade and aiding in the preservation of valuable underwater heritage. The successful integration of multiple exploration techniques and advanced GIS analysis demonstrates a robust framework for future underwater archaeological investigations.

articleTitle: An Experimental Study on a Precise Positioning System with a Correction Guidance Method for Underwater Vehicles
abstract: This research try to create a navigation application that integrates a precise positioning system with a correction guidance method for underwater vehicles. The proposed solution enhances practical exploration by allowing these vehicles to navigate and control themselves accurately within a three-dimensional underwater environment. Underwater vehicles depend on accurate positioning systems to move efficiently underwater. However, traditional satellitebased positioning systems, such as GPS, are not effective in the underwater environment due to its unique conditions. These challenges include difficulties with transmitting radiofrequency signals, problems with light absorption, and the limited effectiveness of machine vision in practical applications. This study has created a correction guidance method for a specialized navigation system designed to address the challenges of underwater exploration, aiming to improve the performance of underwater vehicles. The research utilizes Ultra-Short Baseline (USBL) acoustic technology for positioning, which includes an underwater locator, a receiving antenna/receiver, a baseline array, and a surface instrument box. To enhance underwater positioning accuracy and address concerns related to the underwater environment, this system integrates with both high-precision satellite positioning (RTK-GPS) and the Marine Geographic Information System (MGIS). This integration allows for the simultaneous collection of accurate underwater positioning data, similar to how GPS works for surface vehicles. The underwater positioning system was converted from a relative coordinate system to an absolute coordinate system using MGIS. High-precision positioning data is achieved through custom-developed application programs (APIs) and a correction guidance method, which simplifies ROV navigation control. In practical experimental testing, this study effectively used underwater vehicle positioning information and spatial geographic data to help ROV operators perform accurate underwater positioning tests at four water intake fence locations, which are at a depth of 63 meters in the reservoir. This experiment successfully gathered valuable images for research work.

articleTitle: Subsea Towed Docking Cone for Launch and Recovery of Autonomous Underwater Vehicles
abstract: The increasing demand for efficient, cost-effective, and safe underwater operations has driven the development of advanced Launch and Recovery Systems (LARS) for Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs). This study presents the concept and functional design of a subsea towed docking mechanism, the Launch and Recovery Device (LARD), which addresses critical challenges in AUV recovery by establishing a secure physical connection underwater. The LARD features a funnel-shaped entrance and a frame with articulated struts equipped with adjustable clamps, allowing it to securely grip AUVs of varying sizes using frictional forces. The functional sequences for launch and recovery are outlined, detailing the system's ability to securely position, lock, and release the AUV while ensuring resilience under diverse environmental conditions. Conducting the docking procedure sufficiently deep below the free surface significantly mitigates the impact of wave-induced motion on the AUV and LARD as wave-induced particle motion diminishes with depth. This study analyses the influence of waves at different water depths using examples in the North and Baltic Sea sourced from the German Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency. The particle velocities were derived using Airy and Laplace wave theory, confirming that nonlinear term were negligible for the present study at the examined conditions. Relevant wave behavior is analyzed based on the distinctions between deep, transitional, and shallow waters.

articleTitle: Research on Underwater Target Attitude Estimation Model Based on Multilayer Neural Networks
abstract: In marine operations and equipment deployment, the attitude measurement of underwater targets is a critical factor in ensuring precision and stability. However, traditional methods are constrained by limitations in real-time performance and adaptability in complex ocean environments, failing to meet the demands for high accuracy. To address these challenges, this study proposes a deep learning model based on multilayer neural networks for classifying and predicting the angles of underwater target attitudes. MATLAB simulations were used to generate sonar echo data for rigid ellipsoid targets, extracting frequency response features under varying aspect ratios and attitude angles to construct a high-quality training dataset. The model architecture comprises an input layer, multiple hidden layers, and classification and regression output layers, enabling simultaneous classification of aspect ratios and prediction of attitude angles. During training, the model's performance was optimized by adjusting hyperparameters such as the number of layers, neurons per layer, activation functions, and learning rates, significantly enhancing prediction accuracy and efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that the model achieves 100% accuracy in classification tasks and minimal error in regression tasks, reflecting excellent generalization and robustness. This research provides an efficient and reliable technical solution for underwater target monitoring and attitude estimation in complex marine environments, laying a solid foundation for further studies in related fields.

articleTitle: A Sensor-Actuator Network Towards the Optimization of Feeding in Marine Aquaculture
abstract: As the aquaculture industry continues to expand, optimization of feeding continues to be a crucial issue in mitigating the environmental and economic impacts of poor feeding management, improving the growth and health of the fish, and keeping the industry sustainable. Recognition of fish-feeding behavior and control systems are important tools for estimating the optimal amount of food to be dispensed. In this paper, we proposed a sensor-actuator network made for fish-feeding behavior recognition using fish-induced flow speed measurements and underwater fish imaging. This system also consists of a feeding control module, a motor control panel board, and a feeding machine to control the feeding. We deployed this system at a fish farm for one month. After collecting data, we trained a model to detect the fish from the video recorded near the surface and compared the results from the flow speed measurements. Similarities between the patterns of the fish count and the flow speed showed some promising results that can be used to optimize fish feeding.

articleTitle: Enhancing Marine Debris Acoustic Monitoring by Optical Flow-Based Motion Vector Analysis
abstract: With the development of coastal construction, a large amount of human-generated waste, particularly plastic debris, is continuously entering the ocean, posing a severe threat to marine ecosystems. The key to effectively addressing plastic pollution lies in the ability to autonomously monitor such debris. Currently, marine debris monitoring primarily relies on optical sensors, but these methods are limited in their applicability to underwater and seafloor areas due to low-visibility constraints. The acoustic camera, also known as high-resolution forward-looking sonar (FLS), has demonstrated considerable potential in the autonomous monitoring of marine debris, as they are unaffected by water turbidity and dark environments. The appearance of targets in sonar images changes with variations in the imaging viewpoint, while challenges such as low signal-to-noise ratio, weak textures, and imaging distortions in sonar imagery present significant obstacles to debris monitoring based on prior class labels. This paper proposes an optical flow-based method for marine debris monitoring, aiming to fully utilize the time series information captured by the acoustic camera to enhance the performance of marine debris monitoring without relying on prior category labels of the targets. The proposed method was validated through experiments conducted in a circulating water tank, demonstrating its feasibility and robustness. This approach holds promise for providing novel insights into the spatial and temporal distribution of debris.
